climate.fall: Shortening stable windows into October
climate.spring: Snow lingers into June at elevation; gully often snow-filled
climate.summer: Warm and mostly dry June-September
climate.winter: Heavy snow, access not maintained
climate.typical: Dry, sunny summers with afternoon thunderstorm potential; wet, snowy winters
climate.forecastZone: East-slope Central Cascades / Stuart Range (Wenatchee NWS point forecast area; NWAC Stevens Pass zone for snow/avalanche conditions)

climate.fall: Shortening weather window; first significant snow can arrive by October
climate.spring: Deep snow typically still covers approach trails and upper slopes into June
climate.summer: Primary climbing window (Jul-Sep); still subject to sudden maritime storms
climate.winter: Heavy snow; Hannegan Pass Road becomes a snow-play/ski-touring area and the trailhead is effectively inaccessible to standard vehicles
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the North Cascades crest: heavy, wet Pacific snowpack in winter and a shorter, more stable window from roughly mid-July through September. This far-north, near-border position keeps snow lingering late on north- and east-facing approach slopes.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly after Labor Day; new snow is possible by late September/October at this elevation.
bySeason.spring: Snow persists on the upper mountain into July; creek and river crossings run high with snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best and most reliable window, July-September, though 2021-22 wildfire activity shows this drainage isn't immune to summer fire closures or smoke.
bySeason.winter: Heavy wet snow loads and avalanche terrain on the approach slopes above Brush Creek/Whatcom Pass; road and trail typically snowbound.

climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (NWAC) forecasts cover the Mount Baker zone of the northern Washington Cascades, which includes this area

climate.typical: Warm, dry summer days with a real chance of building afternoon cumulus and thunderstorms, especially July-August; snow can linger in the col/gully well into July on this north-facing approach.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes Central Cascades / Stuart Range zone

climate.fall: September can be superb — cold, stable, snow-free rock — but the first autumn fronts return unpredictably and the days shorten fast on a route with a long approach.
climate.spring: Deep, consolidating snow on the Constance Pass traverse and in the Home Creek basin; the buttress is verglassed and the approach is a snow-travel exercise. Not a practical season for the rock route.
climate.summer: Pacific high pressure gives the clearest and driest spell of the year, and this is the only realistic window for the buttress. Afternoon build-up and marine push can still bring cloud onto the face with little warning.
climate.winter: Heavy wet snow, high avalanche danger across the Constance massif, and a snowbound approach. The buttress is not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Pacific fronts stall against the eastern Olympic wall and produce orographic precipitation, but the Constance massif sits toward the drier eastern rain shadow, so it is noticeably less wet than the Hoh side. Persistent low cloud is the defining nuisance rather than rain.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Olympics avalanche and mountain-weather zone; point forecast for Mount Constance (2,360 m), the adjacent higher summit

climate.fall: September can offer cold, stable, snow-free rock, but returning fronts and shortening days squeeze the margin on a route with a long approach.
climate.spring: Snow and verglas on the northwest face and a snow-covered Constance Pass approach. Not a season for this line.
climate.summer: Pacific high pressure gives the clearest, driest and warmest spell — the only realistic window. Marine cloud can still arrive quickly.
climate.winter: Snowbound approach, high avalanche danger across the massif, and a face plastered in snow and ice. Not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with orographic Pacific precipitation; the Constance massif sits in the drier eastern Olympic rain shadow, but persistent low cloud on the peaks is the norm and is the practical limiting factor for this route.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Olympics zone; point forecast for Mount Constance (2,360 m)

climate.typical: Wet, cool west-slope Cascades climate; heavy winter snowpack persists into early summer, especially on north-facing terrain. Reliable snow-free scrambling conditions typically arrive by late July/August and hold through September.

bySeason.fall: Late September into October: shorter days and rising storm risk; snow can return to the high basin by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Not viable — approach trail and route are largely snow-covered with high avalanche hazard on surrounding slopes during May-June snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best window (August-September): warm, mostly snow-free ridge, though the boulder-field approach still demands care and route-finding.
bySeason.winter: The Foss River roads and the trail are typically snow-covered and effectively inaccessible; not a winter objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass / Stevens Pass zones (the peak sits near the boundary) — check both for early- and late-season travel

climate.typical: East-of-the-crest rain-shadow climate: hot, dry summers with a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms building over the exposed upper ridge, and lingering snow on shaded sections of the trail into late June in heavy-snow years.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Cascade East Central (relevant mainly for early/late-season snow travel, not the core July–Oct scrambling window)

climate.fall: September is good - the Skoogs' variation went on 23 September. Dry rock and stable air, but shortening days on a long route.
climate.spring: Snow-covered and best left alone; the glacier approach is avalanche terrain and the highway is often still gated.
climate.summer: The season opens in mid-July, matching the first-ascent date. Expect residual snow in the ridge's gullies early in the month.
climate.winter: Not a documented winter objective; the highway is closed and the route would be a serious expedition.
climate.typical: East-of-crest North Cascades weather: drier and more continental than the Skagit valley, but Pacific fronts wrap around Ross Lake with little warning. The east aspect gets early sun, which helps dry the rock but also warms any residual snow.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North is the nearest named avalanche zone, though Jack lies east of NWAC's observation network.

climate.fall: Broken glacier and bare ice; not a viable objective on this aspect.
climate.spring: The season. A cold window in May offers the best combination of long days, a filled-in bergschrund and a stable snowpack; parties consistently report that early May beats late May and that June is too late.
climate.summer: The bergschrund opens, the glacier breaks up and the headwall loses its snow. Not the season for this route, though the mountain's south side comes into condition.
climate.winter: Documented winter ascents exist (including a late-January climb), but they involve biking and skiing in from the highway gate, mixed climbing through a cliff band, and full avalanche and cornice hazard management.
climate.typical: A deep, shaded, north-facing cirque that holds winter conditions long after the south side of the mountain has dried out. Cold clear nights give the overnight refreeze the route depends on.
climate.forecastZone: For avalanche information NWAC's West Slopes North is the nearest named zone; because this is a spring snow route on a big north face, the NWAC forecast plus your own observations of overnight refreeze are the operative data.

climate.fall: September gives the driest rock but short days on a long route with a committing descent.
climate.spring: Deep snow and avalanche terrain on the approach; the highway is often still gated. Not the season for the ridge.
climate.summer: The window opens late July, matching the 1 August first ascent and the 22 July date of the best-known modern ascent. Expect residual snow in north-facing gullies.
climate.winter: Not a documented winter objective on this ridge; winter activity on the north side has been on the Nohokomeen headwall.
climate.typical: A shaded north aspect that stays cold and holds snow far longer than the sunny south side of the peak; the Ross Lake corridor funnels Pacific weather in with little warning.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North is the nearest named avalanche zone.

climate.fall: Bare, broken glacier ice and open crevasses; not the season for this line.
climate.spring: Prime season for the north-side glaciers, but the highway is often still gated and the approach involves deep snow and avalanche terrain in the timber and cliff bands.
climate.summer: The glacier opens up quickly through June and July; the 1978 first ascent went on 19 July, but that is late for a filled-in schrund.
climate.winter: Highway closed and full winter conditions. Winter ascents on this side of the mountain have been made via the Nohokomeen headwall, at considerable effort.
climate.typical: North-facing cirques on Jack hold winter conditions far longer than the sunny south side and stay cold and shaded through the morning even in midsummer.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC's West Slopes North is the closest named avalanche zone, though Jack is east of NWAC's observation sites.

climate.typical: Typical North Cascades alpine climate: cool nights even in summer, rapid weather changes, and a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms building over the peaks in July-August.

bySeason.fall: September: often the most stable, clear weather for climbing, with the face fully snow-free; first snow can arrive by late September/October.
bySeason.spring: Snowbound; SR-20 access is typically still gated.
bySeason.summer: July-August: warmest, driest window overall, but also peak thunderstorm season on the east-slope crest; the south-facing rock can still hold snow into July.
bySeason.winter: SR-20 closed; the peak is essentially inaccessible without a very long ski/snowshoe approach.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ301 (Cascades of Whatcom and Skagit Counties)

climate.fall: August and September give the driest rock and the most stable weather. Late September storms leave the greenstone verglassed and greasy.
climate.spring: Snowbound and inaccessible; SR 20 is usually still gated and the Jerry Glacier traverse is avalanche terrain.
climate.summer: July can still hold snow in the ridge's gullies and cracks; mosquitoes are severe at Jerry Lakes. Conditions become reliable through August.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; the highway is closed and the route would be a full alpine expedition.
climate.typical: East-of-crest North Cascades weather - drier and more continental than the Skagit valley, but exposed to Pacific fronts that wrap around Ross Lake. Summer high pressure gives hot, dry rock on the southeast aspect.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC's West Slopes North is the nearest named avalanche zone, but Jack lies well east of NWAC's observation network so treat any avalanche forecast as extrapolation.

climate.fall: August and September are the window - dry rock, no bugs, stable weather, at the cost of carrying water.
climate.spring: Snow-covered with a long snow traverse to Jack's base; the highway is often still gated.
climate.summer: Melts out early relative to the rest of the mountain, but the Class 4 ridge above still wants to be dry, and water on the crest becomes scarce.
climate.winter: Not a documented winter objective; the highway is closed and the traverse would be a major undertaking.
climate.typical: The Little Jack crest is a sunny, exposed, southwest-facing ridge - it dries and melts out earlier than any other approach to the peak, and it bakes in summer.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North is the closest named avalanche zone, relevant only outside the summer season.

NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone — daily NWAC avalanche forecasts run mid-November through mid-April, so for the typical late-April–June climbing window rely on recent trip reports and NPS road and trail condition updates once the regular forecast season ends.

climate.typical: High alpine, east-of-crest-leaning climate on Ragged Ridge: drier and more sun-exposed than the western North Cascades passes, but still subject to fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and afternoon thunderstorms in summer.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in the basins by late September/early October; shortening daylight and early-season snow become the main concerns.
bySeason.spring: Approach slopes and much of the trail are typically still snow-covered; SR 20 itself may not yet be open to the trailhead.
bySeason.summer: Prime window is August-September; July can still hold steep, consequential snow in the summit gully. Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning are a real hazard on the exposed upper ridge and summit block.
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible — SR 20 is gated for the season and the approach is avalanche terrain.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues forecasts only mid-November through mid-April, so there is no formal avalanche forecast covering this route's normal (summer) climbing season.

climate.spring: Deep snowpack and the access road often still gated; high avalanche/wet-slide hazard.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season (Jul-Sep); frequent afternoon thunderstorms and ongoing icefall off the hanging glaciers.
climate.winter: Road closed at a lower gate; extreme avalanche and icefall hazard.
climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters and warmer, drier summers typical of the west-slope North Cascades; the Johannesburg cirque holds hanging glaciers year-round, so cold microclimates and active icefall persist even in summer.
climate.forecastZone: NWS/NWAC "West Slopes North Cascades and Passes" zone (WAZ567)

climate.spring: Cold with variable stability; favored by ski mountaineers for corn-snow conditions on the south face in April-June.
climate.summer: July-September brings the most reliable high-pressure weather windows and best glacier travel conditions.
climate.winter: Heavy snow, avalanche hazard, and very difficult access; rarely climbed.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the North Cascades high country: heavy winter snowpack and wet conditions, with a relatively dry, stable window from mid-July through September. West-facing slopes and glaciers here receive high precipitation, especially as winter snowfall.

bySeason.fall: Early September can still be good, but new snow can arrive by late September/October, re-covering crevasses and making route-finding across the glaciers harder.
bySeason.spring: April can offer firm corn-snow conditions on the south/southeast face for ski mountaineers, but the bergschrund and crevasses are still snow-covered and less predictable; watch for avalanche hazard on approach slopes.
bySeason.summer: July–September is the primary climbing window — glaciers are most open (more visible crevasse hazard but more predictable bridges), rock is driest, and the bergschrund step is climbable.
bySeason.winter: Essentially inaccessible for normal climbing; deep snow, avalanche hazard, and the long approach make winter ascents rare and expedition-style.

climate.typical: Cool, changeable Cascades alpine weather; the gap and lakes basin commonly hold snow into July, and afternoon thunderstorms/humid buildups are common in late summer.

bySeason.fall: Good, often clear conditions into September and early October; nights are cold and the first snow can arrive by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Lower Necklace Valley (to Jade/Emerald Lakes) is typically snow-free by June, but the gap, summit gully, and La Bohn Creek boot path usually still hold significant snow — expect an ice axe and possibly traction.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the summit scramble; trip reports cluster in August.
bySeason.winter: Not a realistic winter objective — deep unbroken snow on the long Necklace Valley approach and avalanche terrain above the gap.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (avalanche/shoulder-season) and NWS King County Cascades forecast zone.

climate.typical: Maritime Cascade snowpack — frequent freeze-thaw, rain-on-snow events, and periods of wind-affected, faceted, or wet-loose snow; check the current NWAC West Slopes South forecast before climbing

climate.typical: Maritime Cascade snowpack with frequent freeze-thaw and rain-on-snow events; check the current NWAC West Slopes South forecast before climbing

climate.typical: Typical wet, unsettled Cascade Crest weather even in midsummer — parties describe overnight rain clearing to sun by morning as a common pattern. Snow can linger in the summit gully and on the glacier remnant into August.

bySeason.spring: Heavy snow lingers into July; expect full glacier-travel gear and potentially difficult, high-volume creek crossings from snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the standard window — Lemah Creek fords are lower and the summit gully is mostly melted to talus/scree by August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone is the nearest official avalanche forecast area, most relevant for late-spring/early-season snow; NWAC does not issue forecasts through the typical July-September climbing season.

climate.fall: Often the most settled rock weather, with the snow finger at its thinnest and the glacier most broken. Days shorten fast on a 20-mile round trip, and the first autumn storms can shut the peak down abruptly.
climate.spring: Deep snowpack on the peak and often on the upper road; the approach trail melts out well before the cirque does, and Lemah Creek runs high. Avalanche season conditions persist in the approach basin.
climate.summer: The reliable window. Pacific high pressure gives long stretches with little or no cloud cover; the snow finger consolidates and the east-facing rock dries. Afternoon convective build-ups are the usual summer hazard.
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall, cloudy conditions and an unplowed access road put the peak effectively out of reach; this is not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Maritime Cascade crest weather. Pacific systems move inland and are forced upward by the crest, producing high precipitation, and the peak sits just far enough east of the divide that conditions can be noticeably drier than at Snoqualmie Pass on the same day.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone is the nearest avalanche forecast area

climate.fall: Excellent. Cool, dry, bug-free and with firm footing; the 1975 documented ascent was on 20-21 September. The window closes with the first substantial snowfall, usually late October or November.
climate.spring: Wet, heavy maritime snowpack and continuing avalanche hazard on both flanks. The road melts out ahead of the mountain, giving a long dry approach to a still-snowbound peak — an awkward combination and the least attractive season on this route.
climate.summer: Snow-free from about early July. The fishing trail to Lichtenwasser Lake is straightforward, the upper slopes are heather and boulder walking, and the ridge is a short easy scramble. Bugs are heavy at the lake in July and August.
climate.winter: The route's headline season and a listed classic backcountry ski tour. Snowfall makes the ridge easy to skin, and the north-facing approach generally holds the better snow. Avalanche hazard is present on both sides of the mountain throughout; consult the NWAC Stevens Pass forecast and reassess continuously in the field.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with heavy Pacific precipitation, predominantly winter snowfall. Just east of the crest, so snow here is typically a little drier and colder than on the west-side slopes, and the north-side approach used by this route holds better quality snow than the sun-exposed south flank.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass avalanche and mountain-weather zone; Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Chelan County

climate.fall: Best conditions of the year — dry rock, cool stable air, no insects. September is the pick; the window closes with the first significant snow, usually in October.
climate.spring: Wet, with lingering snow at the base and on the approach into June. Not a realistic season for the face.
climate.summer: Dry and warm from about early July. Afternoon sun on the west aspect makes hot days uncomfortable and cool days pleasant. Mosquitoes at Lake Valhalla are severe in July and August.
climate.winter: The mountain becomes a ski and snowshoe objective and this face is out of condition. Avalanche hazard is present on both flanks; NWAC's Stevens Pass forecast covers the zone.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with high Pacific-driven precipitation, mostly winter snow. Sitting just east of the crest, the wall dries faster after storms than west-side crags at the same elevation and holds afternoon and evening sun on its west aspect.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass mountain-weather zone; Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Chelan County

climate.fall: The best window. September and October bring cool, drier, largely bug-free conditions and fall colour, with the caveat that the first significant snow can arrive any time from mid-October. The original ascent of the west face and rib was on 21 October.
climate.spring: Deep snow persists on the mountain well after FR 6700 melts out. Avalanche hazard remains real on the north and south flanks into late spring, and the maritime snowpack is wet and heavy. Not a good time for the rock — expect verglas, wet heather and unconsolidated snow in the chutes.
climate.summer: Snow-free from roughly early July. The west face bakes in afternoon sun and is dry and stable then. Mosquitoes and biting insects are severe at Lake Valhalla in July and into August — a party in August reported 100% DEET was ineffective. Afternoon thunderstorms are possible but less common than on the west side.
climate.winter: Lichtenberg's main season, but as a ski and snowshoe peak rather than a rock climb. Snowfall makes skinning the northeast and southeast ridges straightforward, while both the north and south flanks present avalanche hazard, the south side occasionally shedding large slides. NWAC's Stevens Pass forecast covers the zone; a north-slope avalanche cycle on Lichtenberg below 5,000 ft has been documented in NWAC observations.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with weather systems arriving off the Pacific. The North Cascades take very high precipitation, most of it as winter snowfall, though Lichtenberg sits just east of the Cascade crest and generally sees slightly drier, colder snow and more sun than the west-side slopes across the pass. Freeze-thaw and heavy snow loading dominate the peak's character.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass avalanche and mountain-weather zone; Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Chelan County

climate.typical: Marine West Coast climate with a heavy winter snowpack; the Southern Pickets hold snow late and have a short, reliable weather window, generally late July through early September, matching this route's listed season.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone covers this area, but NWAC only issues avalanche/mountain weather forecasts from roughly mid-November through mid-April — outside that window, check NWS point forecasts and recent trip reports for current conditions.

climate.fall: Generally out of condition — old snow gone, new snow not yet consolidated, and the Green Creek approach back to brush and boulders. Not a recommended window for this line.
climate.spring: The prime window for this route. April-May typically offers a consolidated snowpack in the couloir, snow cover over the brushy lower Green Creek approach, and lengthening daylight — but the FR 38 gate at Wallace Creek is generally still closed, so expect extra road miles on foot or bike. Wet-slab and loose-wet avalanche problems develop on south aspects as the day warms.
climate.summer: The couloir goes out of condition. Snow retreats, moats open, and the south side becomes loose rock. Summer is rock-route season on this peak; see the West Face, North Face and Southeast Ridge.
climate.winter: Climbable but serious. One party did it on 31 January 2015 in hard-snow conditions and suspected it was a first winter ascent. Short days force a dark exit, the unbridged river crossing is at its most unpleasant, and the Green Creek basin carries a full avalanche problem. Consult the NWAC West Slopes North forecast.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with very high winter precipitation. Most weather systems arrive off the Pacific and hit the Twin Sisters before Mount Baker, so the range takes the brunt of incoming fronts. Drainage is into the Middle Fork Nooksack via Green, Sister, Skookum and Howard creeks.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (Mt Baker area). NWAC issues daily avalanche and mountain weather forecasts from roughly mid-November through mid-April.

climate.typical: Alpine climate on the east side of the Rainier massif: cold nights even in midsummer (often below freezing at the 7,000+ ft high camp), rapid cloud buildup, and afternoon thunderstorms are common — the massif generates its own severe weather that can arrive with little warning.

bySeason.summer: July-Aug is the primary season: daytime highs in the 50s-60s F at high camp with a hard overnight refreeze early season, transitioning to soft, sun-cupped snow and more rockfall by late August.

climate.forecastZone: Not covered by NWAC avalanche forecasts (NWAC only issues forecasts for terrain below about 8,000 ft, and only late November-mid April); use the NWS Seattle mountain/zone forecast and recent trip reports for current glacier and rockfall conditions.

climate.fall: Cool and often clear, with larch color in nearby basins by late September, but increasing chance of early-season snow.
climate.spring: Snowbound through at least June at these elevations; access road/trails typically not clear until late June.
climate.summer: Warm to hot days with cool nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common in the high country.
climate.winter: Heavy snow and cold; the peak and access roads are effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Dry, sunnier east-slope-Cascades climate compared to the west side, but still exposed and cold at elevation — expect cold nights and possible summer thunderstorms even in August. Snow can linger on north aspects and passes into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in Eureka Creek/Shellrock Basin in late September, but one late-September trip found the high ridges already snowy, cold and wind-blasted — treat late season as shoulder winter conditions.
bySeason.spring: Passes and approach trails are typically snow-covered and not practical for this route.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the high passes (Rolo, Shellrock, Butte); a normal winter clears most routes by early-mid July.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — Harts Pass Road and interior trails are snowbound and the wilderness is essentially inaccessible.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ049 (Western Okanogan County), which covers the Mazama/Winthrop/Twisp/Pasayten area

climate.fall: October is the driest and most stable month here and is when the route was first climbed, at the cost of short days and early darkness on an east-facing wall.
climate.spring: Wet, snowbound on the upper mountain and not in condition. Off-trail approach terrain is buried or rotten.
climate.summer: July through September gives the most daylight and the best odds of a dry spell. Morning sun on the east face is welcome early in the day and can make afternoon starts unpleasantly cold.
climate.winter: Out of condition; the face ices and the off-trail approaches are avalanche and cliff-band terrain.
climate.typical: Maritime west-slope Cascades: heavy precipitation, frequent low cloud, and rock that dries slowly. An east aspect gets morning sun and goes into shade in the afternoon, so it dries faster than the north face but cools off early.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes Central (west-side Cascades along and south of US 2, covering the Skykomish valley near Index and Baring); NOAA Seattle and Mountain-Forecast for Baring Mountain.

climate.fall: Often the nicest time: cool temperatures on a very steep climb, dry ground, and clear air for the summit views. Snow returns to the gully by late October and daylight shortens quickly against a long day.
climate.spring: The upper mountain is a snow climb. The basin and summit gully hold continuous snow and the headwall below the notch is steep; an ice axe is recommended and avalanche hazard needs checking. The forested path below is muddy and slick, and blowdown is common after winter.
climate.summer: Prime season once the snow softens and clears — long daylight, generally stable weather, and the best odds of a dry descent path. Carry plenty of water; there is none above the lower creek crossings and the upper basin is exposed and hot.
climate.winter: A serious undertaking rather than a scramble. The path is buried, the gully is avalanche terrain, and the descent forest is dangerous. Not recommended without full winter mountaineering skills and a current avalanche forecast.
climate.typical: Maritime west-slope Cascades — wet, mild and often cloudy, with the mountain frequently in cloud even when the valley is clear. Because the route is low (2,280 ft trailhead) and steep, conditions change fast with elevation, and the summit can be in wind and cloud when the parking lot is warm.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes Central (west-side Cascades along and south of US 2, including the Skykomish valley near Index and Baring). Use NOAA Seattle and Mountain-Forecast for Baring Mountain for freezing level and precipitation.

climate.fall: September is often the driest and most stable month of the year here and is when the route was first climbed, but daylight is shrinking fast against a fourteen-pitch route plus a three-hour descent. By October the wall is generally wet and the first snows dust the summit ridge.
climate.spring: Wet and unsettled. The approach hillside and the couloirs below the wall carry rotten, sliding snow and running meltwater, and avalanche hazard persists on the steep north-side slopes and in the descent gully. The rock routes are effectively out; the standard northwest-ridge scramble becomes a snow climb.
climate.summer: The only reliable window. July and August bring the longest days and the best odds of a multi-day dry spell, but afternoon convection over the Cascade crest can build thunderstorms with little warning. Freezing levels are high and the face is snow-free.
climate.winter: Out of condition as a rock climb. The face ices, the approach slopes are avalanche terrain, and the descent forest is treacherous. The north face has had a winter ascent (Peter Doorish and Dale Farnham made the first winter ascent of the Cooper-Gordon line in 1984) but that is a serious alpine undertaking, not a variation on the summer climb.
climate.typical: Classic maritime west-slope Cascades: heavy annual precipitation, frequent low cloud, and rock that dries slowly. The north face is shaded and holds moisture far longer than a south aspect, so climbable conditions require an extended dry period rather than a single clear day.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes Central (the west-side zone along and south of US Highway 2, covering the Skykomish valley, Index and Baring); NOAA Seattle point forecast and Mountain-Forecast for Baring Mountain for freezing level and precipitation timing.

climate.fall: Possible but colder, shorter days
climate.spring: Likely too snow-covered
climate.summer: Prime season
climate.winter: Not viable
climate.typical: Best when snow-free in mid-late summer
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades National Park / Washington Pass area

climate.fall: Prime season — face firms to neve/ice, especially late Sept-Oct
climate.spring: Face often still buried/unstable
climate.summer: Often too soft/rotten to protect well
climate.winter: Buried; avalanche hazard high
climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters and a short summer dry window typical of the western Cascade crest
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades National Park (nearby NWAC Cascade Pass zone)

climate.fall: Good into September if dry
climate.spring: Wet — snowmelt/seepage on lower pitches
climate.summer: Prime season; hot, early start recommended
climate.winter: Highway 20 access closed by seasonal gate
climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-side Cascades summer; full south-facing sun most of the day
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades east-side (use NWAC for the pass)

climate.fall: Fall (September-November) sees increasing snow, wind, and storms. Not typically climbed due to short daylight, unpredictable weather, and early seasonal storms. Possible light snow cover.
climate.spring: Spring (March-May) is the best climbing season. Snow consolidates into corn, and stable avalanche conditions prevail. Daytime temperatures rise to 25-35°F. May sees increasingly wet conditions and rain-on-snow avalanche hazard. Late spring brings loose rock and wet gully sections.
climate.summer: Summer (June-September) features melted gully sections, exposed wet rock, and severe brush. Avalanche hazard decreases but rockfall increases. Temperatures rise to 45-60°F. Afternoon thunderstorms are common and dangerous on exposed ridge.
climate.winter: Winter (December-February) features deep, stable snow, but extreme cold, high avalanche hazard from new snow, and frequent storms. Temperatures drop to 10-25°F. Days are short (8 hours daylight). Early-season (December-January) snow depth can exceed 10 feet at higher elevations.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Orographic lift forces Pacific weather systems upward, creating high precipitation. Temperatures on the peak typically range from 20-35°F in winter, 25-40°F in spring. Wind is frequent and can be extreme, especially on the summit ridge.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Cascade Crest (CAS), specifically lower west-slope Cascades near Stevens Pass Zone

climate.fall: Wet and stormy with short days. The north face plasters with verglas after the first autumn systems and rarely comes back into condition before winter.
climate.spring: Deep snow, real avalanche hazard in the approach couloir and on the glacier, and a gated road far below the trailhead. Skiers use this cirque in spring, but as a climb it is a large undertaking with a long road approach.
climate.summer: Late June to early August gives the best combination: snow-covered glacier, bridged bergschrund, and an open road. By late summer the glacier goes to bare ice at its margins and the schrund opens.
climate.winter: Full winter conditions — heavy snow, frequent avalanches on the steep terrain of the basin, road closed. A ski-mountaineering objective rather than a climb.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with high precipitation, mostly snow in winter, and wet heavy maritime snow. This north-facing cirque holds winter conditions far longer than the peak's south side and can be in full snow-and-ice condition when the South Ridge is dry heather.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 — West Slopes of the North Cascades and Passes. Consult NWAC for avalanche conditions on the west slopes of the north Cascades whenever snow is present, which on this aspect is most of the useful season.

climate.fall: Out of condition — wet, stormy, and short-dayed, with no reliable snow in the couloir until winter rebuilds it.
climate.spring: The season. Firm overnight freezes give supportable snow at dawn and the couloir softens through the morning; reports describe 'great corn' on the lower descent and heavy sluffing once the sun is on the line. Rime growth of several inches has been noted on exposed ridges in this cirque.
climate.summer: The line thins and the finish becomes the published 'rock' option, with a loose funnel and open glacier below. The window generally closes by late June or early July.
climate.winter: Full winter snowpack and frequent avalanche cycles in these cirques; the road is closed and the approach is a multi-day undertaking.
climate.typical: Maritime west-side climate with a deep, heavy snowpack. This northeast-facing cirque holds winter conditions long after the peak's south side has melted out, which is exactly why the couloir is a spring rather than a summer objective.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 — West Slopes of the North Cascades and Passes. Check the NWAC avalanche forecast covering the west slopes of the north Cascades every day this route is in condition; it is a snow climb in avalanche season.

climate.fall: Fine light and empty terrain but wet, windy and short-dayed. A northwest-facing Class 4 route that has taken autumn rain may not dry again that season.
climate.spring: Stormy and wet with a gated road far below the trailhead; the approach slopes are avalanche terrain and the climb is out of condition.
climate.summer: Mid-July to early September is the window. Snow is off all but the highest ground by July; expect settled spells punctuated by afternoon convection over the surrounding peaks.
climate.winter: Deep maritime snowpack, frequent avalanches on the steep terrain around Cascade Pass, road closed.
climate.typical: Wet-side maritime climate: high precipitation, heavy wet snow in winter, and a genuinely short reliable summer window. The northwest aspect stays shaded and damp longer than the south side of the same peak.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 — West Slopes of the North Cascades and Passes; NWAC for avalanche conditions when snow is present.

climate.fall: Wet, windy, short days. A dusting of new snow on dry heather is worse than either bare heather or a proper snowpack.
climate.spring: Wet and stormy with a gated road. The cirque is full avalanche terrain and the gullies are loaded.
climate.summer: The season, and the aspect that comes into condition first. July gives snow-filled gullies and firm travel; August gives dry, loose gullies and hot afternoons.
climate.winter: Deep maritime snow, frequent avalanches on the steep terrain around Cascade Pass, road closed.
climate.typical: Maritime west-side climate: high precipitation, heavy wet winter snow, and a genuinely short settled summer. The southwest aspect of this cirque melts out early and bakes in the afternoon.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 — West Slopes of the North Cascades and Passes; NWAC for avalanche conditions when snow is present.

climate.fall: Cold, clear spells can give excellent friction, but the schrund is at its most open and the days are short for the approach involved. First autumn storms end the season quickly on this aspect.
climate.spring: Wet, stormy, gated road, loaded approach slopes. The route is out of condition and the schrund is buried.
climate.summer: Mid-July to mid-August balances a still-bridged bergschrund against dry rock. Afternoon sun on the west face helps it dry but also makes the pocket glacier soft for the return.
climate.winter: Deep maritime snowpack and frequent avalanches around the Cascade Pass cirques; road closed.
climate.typical: Maritime west-side climate — high precipitation, wet heavy winter snow, and a short settled summer window. A west-facing rock route at 7,000 ft here needs a genuine dry spell, not just a dry day.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 — West Slopes of the North Cascades and Passes; NWAC for avalanche conditions when snow is present on the approach.

climate.fall: Glaciers exposed as bare/blue ice by September, requiring ice screws in places
climate.spring: Deep snowpack with well-bridged but hidden crevasses after fresh snowfall
climate.summer: Prime climbing season; approach trail largely snow-free by August, glacier travel remains necessary all season
climate.winter: Heavy snow, avalanche hazard, and a closed access road — essentially unclimbed this season
climate.typical: Cool, wet, and often cloudy; the Eldorado Icecap generates its own localized weather that can diverge sharply from valley forecasts
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes)

climate.fall: Glaciers bare ice by September
climate.spring: Deep snowpack, hidden crevasses; steep exposed firn on the approach slope
climate.summer: Main season; approach largely snow-free by August though the ridge approach slope may hold firn longer
climate.winter: Road closed, avalanche terrain
climate.typical: Cool, wet, changeable icecap weather
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes)

climate.fall: Good into September if dry
climate.spring: Snow/wet conditions in the approach gully likely
climate.summer: Prime season
climate.winter: Highway 20 access closed by seasonal gate
climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-side Cascades summer
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades east-side (use NWAC for the pass)

climate.fall: Good into September if dry
climate.spring: Snow lingers in the approach gully; not recommended
climate.summer: Prime season
climate.winter: Highway 20 access closed by seasonal gate
climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-side Cascades summer; south-facing wall gets full sun
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades east-side (use NWAC for the pass)

climate.fall: Good climbing into September if weather holds; shortening days and cooling temps
climate.spring: Snow and meltwater linger in the approach gully; not recommended
climate.summer: Prime season; hot on the south-facing wall, water available near the base into early September
climate.winter: Highway 20 access closed by seasonal gate
climate.typical: Dry, sunny summers typical of the east-side Cascades; the south-facing wall gets sun most of the day
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades east-side (use NWAC for the pass)

climate.fall: September-October: Early season storms; generally climbable with shorter daylight.
climate.spring: May-June: Melting snow, variable conditions, avalanche danger with wet snow. Snow covers lower brush.
climate.summer: July-August: Driest season. Less snow, rock climbing more exposed, but summer rockfall hazard increases. Water scarcity potential.
climate.winter: November-April: Heavy snow, wet conditions, avalanche danger. Traverse more complex with snow routing.
climate.typical: Maritime west coast with abundant precipitation. Snow tends to be wet and heavy, creating avalanche hazard.
climate.forecastZone: National Weather Service Seattle - Puget Sound and Hood Canal zone

climate.fall: Most settled season.
climate.spring: Nearby creek/bridge crossing can run high.
climate.summer: Warm/dry, cooler than Walla Walla.
climate.winter: Occasional access during inversions; road plowed for Bluewood.
climate.typical: Dry summers, cold snowy winters; Minidike sits ~3,712 ft.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Pendleton, WAZ030 (Northwest Blue Mountains of Washington)

climate.fall: Difficult conditions from September onward; not recommended outside July-August.
climate.spring: Snow-covered approach; trail not clear until late June.
climate.summer: Best climbing July-August. July highs 65-75F at base camp, 40-50F on peaks. August similar with increasing instability. Most snow gone by late July.
climate.winter: Not practical; requires advanced winter mountaineering.
climate.typical: Alpine climate with rapid weather changes. Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August. Temperatures at 8,200 ft range 40-60F. High UV index.
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades alpine zone; consult NWAC

climate.fall: Stable weather can persist into September/early October before the highway closes for winter; nights turn cold.
climate.spring: Snow and cool temperatures linger into June at this elevation; SR-20 itself often doesn't reopen for the season until April or May.
climate.summer: Prime season, late June through September; hot, dry days with afternoon convective storm risk.
climate.winter: SR-20 is closed and unplowed; the peak is essentially inaccessible by normal means.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny alpine summer days with a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms; the East Face gets morning-to-early-afternoon sun (roughly 6am-2pm) then goes into shade.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Western Okanogan County mountain zone / NWAC Washington Pass mountain-weather zone

climate.fall: Most settled season.
climate.summer: Warm/dry, cooler than Walla Walla.
climate.winter: Occasional access during inversions; road plowed for Bluewood.
climate.typical: Dry summers, cold snowy winters.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Pendleton, WAZ030 (Northwest Blue Mountains of Washington)

climate.fall: Route becomes difficult in September; snow returns to higher passes. Not recommended outside July-August.
climate.spring: Snow-covered approach in May; trail not reliably clear until late June.
climate.summer: Best climbing window. July averages highs 65-75F at base camp, 40-50F on peaks. August similar with increasing instability. Frequent afternoon thunderstorms. Most snow gone by late July.
climate.winter: Route is not practical in winter; approach requires advanced winter mountaineering skills.
climate.typical: Alpine climate with rapid weather changes. Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August. Temperatures at 8,200 ft range 40-60F. High UV index due to elevation and glacier reflection.
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades alpine zone; high-elevation weather forecasts from NWAC

climate.fall: Snow can return as early as late September/October, shortening the climbing window quickly.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack with high avalanche/wet-slide hazard on approach slopes and the glacier; route generally not in condition
climate.summer: Prime season (Jul-Sep); afternoon thunderstorms and lightning are possible; the Terror Glacier holds firm snow into mid-summer most years
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — approach access and avalanche hazard make the route effectively closed
climate.typical: Wet, maritime North Cascades climate at lower elevations transitioning to persistent snow/glacier conditions above ~6,000'; brush and blowdown dominate the lower approach
climate.forecastZone: No dedicated summer alpine forecast zone exists; NWAC's West Slopes North zone covers this area for winter avalanche forecasting (mid-Nov to mid-Apr) only

climate.fall: Snow can return as early as late September/October, quickly closing the window.
climate.spring: Continuous snow cover on the glacier and gully; ski/splitboard descents of the upper West Ridge have been reported in late April with corn-snow conditions.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season; glacier crossing softens and the gully can melt out to loose rock/scree by late summer.
climate.winter: Deep snowpack and avalanche terrain make the route effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Big diurnal swings are typical: warm, sun-exposed scrambling on the ridge by midday, but near-freezing temperatures and firm snow at the 7,200 ft col in early morning. Afternoon thunderstorm build-up is common on hot August days in the North Cascades interior, so an early start matters.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ301 (Cascades of Whatcom & Skagit Counties) is the relevant mountain-weather zone; NWAC does not forecast avalanche danger for the Pickets and only operates roughly mid-November through June anyway.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: heavy, wet snow accumulates through winter on the approach slopes, and the Mixup Arm snowfield/glacier crossing typically isn't reliably safe until mid-to-late July, with snow sometimes lingering on face ledges into August in a heavy year. Summers are generally stable under the Pacific high, but afternoon cumulus buildup and thunderstorms occur; check NWAC and the NPS backcountry conditions page before committing to the glacier crossing.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes Central (mountain weather zone) / NPS North Cascades backcountry conditions page

climate.fall: Cooling, early snow possible by October
climate.spring: Snow lingers into June on the shaded NE aspect
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window; watch for afternoon storms
climate.winter: SR-20 closed; peak inaccessible without a heavy ski/snowshoe approach
climate.typical: Dry, warm summers with afternoon thunderstorm potential
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades East (NWS mountain forecast zone)

climate.fall: Cooling, early snow possible by October
climate.spring: Snow lingers into June on the shaded NE aspect
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window; watch for afternoon storms
climate.winter: SR-20 closed; peak inaccessible without a heavy ski/snowshoe approach
climate.typical: Dry, warm summers with afternoon thunderstorm potential
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass / North Cascades East (NWS mountain forecast zone)

climate.fall: Narrow window into September before early-season snow returns; little documented activity
climate.spring: Heavy residual snow on approach and glacier; not climbed
climate.summer: Primary season (Jul-Aug)
climate.winter: Inaccessible; no winter ascents documented
climate.typical: Dry, warm alpine summers with a short climbing season; afternoon thunderstorms common
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ048 - Western Chelan County (NWS Spokane/OTX)

climate.fall: Good into September.
climate.spring: Snow and wet rock possible; dries quickly once winter snowpack clears.
climate.summer: Prime season, though shaded until ~1 PM daily.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate; west aspect stays cool/shaded until early afternoon.
climate.forecastZone: NWS 'West Slopes North Central Cascades and Passes' zone (WAZ568)

climate.fall: Good into September.
climate.summer: Prime season.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the west-slope Cascades.
climate.forecastZone: NWS 'West Slopes North Central Cascades and Passes' zone (WAZ568)

climate.fall: Good into September before weather turns.
climate.spring: Steep snow can linger on the approach talus; route dries fast once clear.
climate.summer: Prime season; sun-drenched SW aspect.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate; SW-facing rock dries and warms quickly once the approach snow is gone.
climate.forecastZone: NWS 'West Slopes North Central Cascades and Passes' zone (WAZ568)

climate.winter: Road to Barlow Pass typically closed by snow; area not accessible
climate.typical: Low-elevation (~2,300-2,360 ft), forested, shaded valley-bottom setting on the west slope of the Cascades near Barlow Pass — consistent with the persistent moss and fern growth on the wall noted by the route developers.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone covering the Cascades of Snohomish County (near WAZ302 'Cascades of Snohomish and Northern King Counties')

climate.typical: The Dosewallips valley sits partly in the Olympics' rain shadow, so it's noticeably drier than the park's west-side rainforest valleys, but weather remains Pacific-driven and can turn wet and socked-in with little warning at any time of year. The upper mountain holds substantial snowpack well into summer.

bySeason.fall: September-October: reliable weather windows shrink, first snow can arrive by late September, and the Flypaper snow finger may be melted out to loose scree, adding difficulty and rockfall exposure.
bySeason.spring: April-May: the lower valley trail is often snow-free, but Honeymoon Meadows, Anderson Pass, and above are typically still under deep winter snowpack; the Flypaper Pass snow finger is usually well-consolidated for climbing or ski mountaineering.
bySeason.summer: Late May through August is the main climbing window — expect mostly settled weather with occasional Pacific frontal systems bringing rain and wind, and increasing bare ice and crevasse/bergschrund exposure on the Eel Glacier as the season progresses.
bySeason.winter: November-March: the permanent road washout plus heavy snowpack make this essentially inaccessible for standard climbing; attempted only by well-equipped ski mountaineers in stable avalanche conditions.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues an 'Olympics' avalanche zone forecast, but only in winter (roughly Nov-Apr); for summer climbing season, use NPS current-conditions pages, recent trip reports, and a point weather forecast rather than NWAC.

climate.typical: Summer base temperatures typically run 50-60°F, dropping steadily with elevation; the mountain's Pacific-facing position brings notoriously fast-changing weather, frequent cloud cap/whiteout conditions, and an average of roughly 50 ft of snowfall per year at elevation — plan for low-visibility navigation even on an otherwise 'good' forecast day.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (avalanche/mountain weather)

climate.fall: Route generally out of condition
climate.spring: Best conditions before bergschrund forms
climate.summer: Bergschrund near the summit approach can become difficult late season
climate.winter: Road closed, inaccessible
climate.typical: South-facing, similar to Easton Glacier but slightly less traveled
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North / Mt. Baker area

climate.fall: Larches near Upper Eagle Lake turn color in late September to mid-October, a popular but late-season window
climate.spring: Snow typically lingers in shaded gullies and on the approach route into June
climate.summer: July–September is the most reliable snow-free climbing window
climate.winter: Access road and trail are snowbound and unmaintained; not a winter objective
climate.typical: East of the Cascade crest in a notably drier, sunnier microclimate than the west-side Cascades. Summers bring warm days (70s-80s F at the trailhead, cooler and breezier on the ridge) with occasional afternoon thunderstorms; winters bring heavy snow that lingers in the shaded Eagle Lakes cirque into midsummer.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Western Okanogan County mountain zone (WAZ049), part of the East Slopes of the North Cascades forecast area

climate.fall: Prime larch season around the Eagle Lakes and the classic time to be in this basin, but the window is short. An October 7 party described it as the last snow-free alpine weekend of the year with snow and storms already coming in. Nights are freezing and days are short.
climate.spring: Snowbound and slow. Snow lingers on FR 4340-300 and the Gold Creek road well into spring — a party in late March had to travel nine miles of snow-covered road on foot with a sled before even starting the trail, and used crampons, snowshoes and skis above. Upper Eagle Lake and the summit slopes hold snow long after the valley melts out.
climate.summer: Hot, dry and stable — the best window. Meadows on the approach can carry heavy mosquito pressure in early summer (an early-July party reported significant mosquito pressure through the meadow sections). Afternoon convection over Sawtooth Ridge is the main summer hazard.
climate.winter: Deep snow, unplowed roads and a genuine expedition-scale approach. Winter ascents have been made — a March party reached the summit from Upper Eagle Lake via 3rd-class rock and snow — but the road walk alone adds nine miles each way, and the East Face rock route is out of the question.
climate.typical: Bigelow sits east of the Cascade crest in the range's rain shadow, so it is markedly drier and more settled than the west-side North Cascades. Weather systems originate over the Pacific and track northeast into the Cascades, dropping most of their moisture on the western slopes before reaching the Methow. Summers are hot and dry; winters are cold and snowy.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ522, 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest'. For winter attempts, NWAC's East Slopes North zone covers the Methow Valley / eastern North Cascades; note NWAC only issues avalanche forecasts during the winter season, so there is no avalanche product during Bigelow's normal July-September climbing window.

climate.fall: Shortening daylight and returning snow by late season.
climate.spring: Glacier and gully approach heavily snow-covered.
climate.summer: Primary season; glacier crossing to the ridge base most passable.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; heavy snow and avalanche terrain.
climate.typical: Wet, marine-influenced North Cascades climate; short reliable summer/fall climbing window.
climate.forecastZone: Nearest NWAC mountain-weather/avalanche zone is the Mount Baker area (West Slopes North)

climate.typical: Dry, sunny summers with cold nights at elevation; the Pasayten sits in a rain shadow east of the Cascade crest and is noticeably drier than the western North Cascades, but afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August.

bySeason.fall: Can offer stable, dry weather into early October, but an early snowfall can close access with little warning.
bySeason.spring: Approach roads and high passes are typically snowbound into June/July — not a realistic climbing window.
bySeason.summer: Prime window is roughly mid-July through September once Freds Pass and Rolo Pass clear of snow; warm days, cold nights, and afternoon convective storms are typical.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible; Harts Pass Road is snow-gated and the approach crosses avalanche terrain.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC does not issue a Pasayten-specific avalanche forecast; use Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / Methow Valley Ranger District trail reports plus a general North Cascades East-side weather forecast.

climate.fall: Often stable, clear weather into September, sometimes early October, but with shorter daylight and the possibility of early-season snow at elevation.
climate.spring: Significant snow persists on the upper approach and at the Clark-Johnson col into June; trail access is generally best from late June onward.
climate.summer: The main climbing window — generally snow-free on the route by July, with warm and sometimes hot afternoon conditions on the sun-exposed south/east ledges.
climate.winter: Deep snowpack effectively closes the approach and route to casual travel; the Recreation.gov reservation season for Royal Basin runs mid-May through mid-October.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the interior Olympics: heavy winter snowpack lingers into July at this elevation, with a short reliable dry window roughly late July through September. The interior Olympics sit partly in a rain shadow relative to the outer coast but still see frequent Pacific frontal systems and can cloud up or get rained on even in midsummer.

bySeason.fall: September into early October can be good, with cooler temps and fewer bugs, but earlier storms/snow are possible and days shorten quickly.
bySeason.spring: Deep snowpack and avalanche-prone approach terrain; Royal Basin is often still snow-covered into June -- not recommended for the scramble.
bySeason.summer: Late July-August is the most reliable window: trail mostly snow-free, though upper gullies and the col approach can still hold snow patches into July.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible for climbing; heavy snow closes the approach and avalanche hazard is high.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC's Olympics zone avalanche forecast (issued in winter and spring) covers this range; for summer trips use the NWS zone forecast for the Olympics and Olympic NP's current-conditions/trip-planning pages instead.

climate.typical: The east-side Olympics sit in a rain shadow, so Constance is notably drier than western peaks like Mount Olympus, but it still catches fast-moving Pacific frontal systems with little warning, and afternoon thunderstorms occur in summer. Snow can linger in Avalanche Canyon and on the Terrible Traverse well into July in heavy-snow years.

bySeason.fall: Good windows persist into late September before early snow returns; shorter daylight demands an earlier start.
bySeason.spring: Full winter/spring snowpack still covers the upper route with avalanche terrain in Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute — not a scrambling objective.
bySeason.summer: Late June through September is the primary climbing window; conditions are usually driest and most reliable in August.
bySeason.winter: Full winter mountaineering conditions with significant avalanche hazard; rarely attempted.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC's 'Olympics' zone (nwac.us) covers this range but is only forecast during snow season — no avalanche bulletin is issued during the typical July-September climbing window, so rely on recent trip reports and the WIC for current snow conditions.

climate.fall: September can still offer good windows but with shortening days.
climate.spring: Deep snowpack persists into early summer.
climate.summer: Late July-August brings the most stable, dry weather.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible due to heavy snow and avalanche hazard.
climate.typical: High alpine North Cascades climate: cool, wet, and snow-heavy much of the year, with a short stable-weather window mid-summer.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ301 - Cascades of Whatcom and Skagit Counties (Seattle/NWS office)

climate.fall: Weather deteriorates and snow returns by roughly early October, matching the point at which NPS backcountry camping fees stop being charged for the season.
climate.spring: Approach passes typically remain heavily snow-covered into June/July, easing brush travel but adding steep-snow and avalanche exposure.
climate.summer: July and the first weeks of August are the most reliably dry and stable; by mid-to-late August nearby glaciers and moats open up and can complicate approach terrain, though the SW Flank itself is non-glaciated.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible for climbing; deep snowpack and avalanche hazard affect all approaches.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast alpine climate typical of the North Cascades crest — heavy winter snowpack, a wet, slow-to-clear spring, and a comparatively drier but still unsettled summer. An unnamed glacier occupies Crowder's north cirque.

bySeason.fall: Early snow and rime can arrive by late September, adding difficulty to the already-loose SW Flank and the NE Ridge's exposed sections.
bySeason.spring: The Chilliwack River ford runs high and cold with snowmelt; upper gullies typically still hold snow.
bySeason.summer: July through September is the historically favorable window for a snow-free SW Flank; the best-documented ascent was made August 12.
bySeason.winter: Deep snowpack and avalanche exposure make the peak essentially inaccessible.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Seattle / NWAC North Cascades — Whatcom/Skagit backcountry zone forecast

climate.summer: Prime climbing window; the Needle Pass approach snow gully typically firms up or melts out by mid-to-late summer.
climate.winter: Heavy, wet maritime snowfall with high avalanche hazard on approach slopes; not a winter objective.
climate.typical: The Olympics see notably more precipitation and cloud cover than the Cascades — even on a forecast-clear day, expect marine cloud layers to sit on the ridge crest and complicate route-finding on the exposed pinnacle. The shared Needle Pass approach couloir typically holds firm, sometimes icy, continuous snow into July (crampons/axe recommended); by August it's often melted out to hardpacked dirt and scree.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' zone (nwac.us) for spring snowpack/avalanche info; no dedicated summer alpine weather zone — use the general NWS Quilcene/Hoodsport point forecast.

climate.typical: The Olympics see notably more precipitation and cloud cover than the Cascades — even on a forecast-clear day, expect marine cloud layers to sit on the ridge crest and complicate summit-area and descent route-finding. The Needle Pass couloir typically holds firm, sometimes icy, continuous snow into July (crampons and an axe are recommended); by August it is often melted out to hardpacked dirt and scree with an open moat where any snow remains.

bySeason.fall: Generally snow-free through mid-September with shortening daylight and increasing storm frequency thereafter.
bySeason.spring: Deep, potentially unstable snow fills the Needle Pass couloir — avalanche terrain; check NWAC before an early-season attempt.
bySeason.summer: The main climbing window (June–September); snow-free rock but foggy mornings/marine cloud on the ridge are common.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — heavy snowpack, avalanche hazard, and very difficult access.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' zone (nwac.us) for spring snowpack/avalanche info; no dedicated summer alpine weather zone — use the general NWS Quilcene/Hoodsport point forecast.

climate.summer: Relatively dry overall but with frequent afternoon thunderstorm buildups, especially in July; this is the main climbing window.
climate.winter: Long, cold, and heavily snowed in; the approach and route are not realistically viable without full winter mountaineering equipment and skills.
climate.typical: One of the wetter, more remote corners of the North Cascades near the Canadian border — expect fast-changing weather and snow lingering into July. There's no dedicated avalanche/weather forecast coverage this far into the Chilliwacks (NWAC's nearest zone, Mt. Baker, doesn't specifically cover this area); check NPS current-conditions pages and recent trip reports rather than relying on a formal zone forecast.
climate.forecastZone: NWS WAZ301 -- Cascades of Whatcom and Skagit Counties

climate.fall: Shortening daylight and increasing storm frequency; early-season snow possible by September/October.
climate.spring: Approach still largely snow-covered; wet, heavy maritime snowpack keeps avalanche danger high.
climate.summer: Primary climbing window; brush dries out and snowfields consolidate by mid-to-late season.
climate.winter: Heavy, wet snowfall, high avalanche hazard, and inaccessible/snowed-in approach road and trail.
climate.typical: Wetter and cloudier than the east-side Cascades due to proximity to Puget Sound weather systems; expect frequent overcast and drizzle even in summer, with lingering snow on shaded aspects into July.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC's 'West Slopes North' zone covers this area, but NWAC only issues avalanche forecasts mid-November through mid-April — there is no avalanche forecast service during the summer climbing season.

climate.fall: Conditions deteriorate quickly after mid-September with increasing rain, wind, and early snow.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack lingers into early summer; the Catwalk and glacier crossing are typically not viable until snow consolidates.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable weather and access window, though rain and wind can still arrive with little warning.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — access roads close seasonally and the range holds a deep, unstable snowpack.
climate.typical: The Bailey Range interior sees more precipitation and cloud cover than the rain-shadow towns north of the park but less than the drenched western river valleys; persistent snowfields commonly linger into July even in average years.

bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window mid-July through early September; best conditions (intact snow bridges, softer sidehill snow) are mid-July to mid-August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues an 'Olympics' avalanche/mountain-weather zone forecast, but NWAC only operates in winter (roughly mid-November through mid-April) — for summer climbing conditions, use NWS point forecasts for the area plus recent trip reports.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy orographic precipitation; interior Olympic cols and north-facing slopes (including the Catwalk) can hold snow well into July. Late July through mid-September is the most reliable snow-free window, though afternoon cloud buildup and thunderstorms are common even in midsummer.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone Area Forecast for the Olympics (WAZ328). NWAC's Olympic Mountains weather forecast runs only seasonally (roughly November-June, avalanche season) and does not cover the typical July-September climbing window for this route.

climate.fall: September can be stable and superb, with firm snow and cold nights, but the glaciers are at their most broken and the first Pacific storms arrive without much warning. October brings genuine winter conditions to the summit.
climate.spring: Wet and heavy. Snow tends to be wet and dense, producing high avalanche danger, and the Access Creek approach is still buried. Travel is technically easier under continuous snow cover but the approach is far longer, and SR 20 is often still gated.
climate.summer: The Pacific high pressure system builds over the region and produces the clearest, driest weather of the year. Valley heat in Big Beaver and Access Creek is oppressive and mosquitoes and biting flies are abundant; high on the mountain the days are long and generally stable. This is the climbing season.
climate.winter: High winter snowfall on the western slopes, wet heavy snow and high avalanche danger. SR 20 is closed and the approach is a multi-day expedition; essentially nobody climbs East Fury in winter.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Weather systems form over the Pacific and track northeast into the Cascades, where the range forces them upward and wrings out heavy orographic precipitation. Fog and low rolling cloud are common even in settled summer weather and can shut down route-finding on the ridge within minutes.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) issues the avalanche forecast for the west-slope North Cascades; NOAA/NWS Seattle issues the point forecast for the Picket Range within North Cascades National Park.

climate.fall: The snow melts back and the lower route becomes a long rock climb, with wide moats and a more awkward bergschrund. Stable Septembers happen, but so do the first big storms - one September attempt on this face was overtaken by heavy snow and stretched from seven days to ten.
climate.spring: Wet, heavy snow and high avalanche danger; the face is loaded and the approach is buried. Not a spring objective.
climate.summer: Pacific high pressure gives the clearest and most stable weather. July leaves much more of the lower route under snow, which historically makes for faster, cleaner climbing; the trade-off is more active rockfall off the hanging glaciers as the day warms.
climate.winter: High snowfall, wet heavy snow, high avalanche danger and a gated highway. Not a winter objective by any reasonable measure.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate, with Pacific systems forced up over the range and dropping heavy orographic precipitation on the western slopes. This is a shaded north face, so it holds snow and cold far later than the southeast side of the mountain.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) issues the avalanche forecast for the west-slope North Cascades; NOAA/NWS Seattle issues the point forecast for the Picket Range within North Cascades National Park.

climate.typical: Warm, relatively dry alpine summer days with a real risk of afternoon thunderstorms; overnight lows near/below freezing at the higher camps and on the glacier.

bySeason.summer: Late June and early July often still have firm, steep snow on the Southeast Glacier and approach heather slopes (a contributing factor in the June 2025 accident); conditions are typically more consolidated and predictable by August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (note: NWAC's public avalanche forecasts are a winter/spring product and do not cover summer glacier-travel conditions on Fury)

climate.fall: Weather deteriorates quickly after early-mid September with returning snow
climate.spring: Heavy, lingering wet snowpack into June/July; high avalanche and stream-crossing hazard on approach
climate.summer: Jul-Aug is the primary climbing season with the most stable weather, though afternoon thunderstorms occur
climate.winter: Heavy wet snow, high avalanche danger, and SR-20 access closed
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with a heavy winter snowpack; the Pickets hold snow late into summer, and the route is rarely reliably snow-free before late July. August is the most common summit month, though brief, intense Cascade thunderstorms are common in late summer and this route offers no fast retreat once on the exposed connecting ridge.

bySeason.fall: By September, glacier crossings become icier and more crevassed, and weather windows shorten significantly.
bySeason.summer: Late July-August is prime season, offering the best balance of consolidated snow on the East Mount Fury Glacier and stable rock; watch for afternoon thunderstorm buildup.

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC avalanche forecast zone covers this cross-country summer climbing objective; check NOAA point forecasts for the Ross Lake/North Cascades backcountry before committing to the traverse.

climate.fall: Cooler, often stable weather through September-October before the road closes for winter; early-season snow is possible.
climate.spring: Snow-covered into June; the road may only just have reopened and the upper mountain still holds a continuous snowpack (good glissade conditions but slough/avalanche hazard on warm days).
climate.summer: Typically snow-free by late July/August; the route becomes a dry, loose Class 2-3 talus scramble that is hot and exposed on the south-facing slopes.
climate.winter: Highway 20 is closed for the season; the peak is essentially inaccessible without a very long approach on foot or skis.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with heavy winter snowfall; summers are drier with clear mornings and a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms/showers, especially July-August.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly; possible early snow, shorter days, and wildfire smoke can linger into September in bad fire years.
bySeason.spring: Road typically reopens April-May; approach still largely snow-covered — good for early snow climbs but watch for wet-slide activity on steep terrain.
bySeason.summer: Best window (July-Sept); talus/scree mostly snow-free, with real afternoon thunderstorm risk.
bySeason.winter: Highway closed; deep snowpack and avalanche terrain on all approach slopes.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes North (Canadian Border to Lake Chelan) for winter/spring avalanche forecasting; check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report for current road status.

climate.fall: Increasingly wet, with early snow possible by October
climate.spring: Wet, with substantial lingering snowpack at and above First Divide into June
climate.summer: Driest, most stable season and the standard climbing/scrambling window
climate.winter: Heavy, wet, maritime snowfall; not a scrambling season and avalanche-prone
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the interior Olympics: Pacific storm systems drive heavy orographic precipitation, with wet, heavy snowfall accumulating at elevation in winter and often lingering into summer at First Divide and above.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC (Northwest Avalanche Center) — Olympics zone, relevant for early-season snow travel on the approach and summit slopes.

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows and rising chance of early snow after September
climate.spring: Heavy residual snowpack on the approach trail and col persists into June
climate.summer: Driest, most stable window (Jul-Sep), though still subject to afternoon thunderstorms
climate.winter: Deep snow, avalanche terrain, and closed/gated access roads; not a winter objective
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Royal Basin and the Needles sit in a partial rain shadow of the higher west-side Olympic peaks, so precipitation is somewhat lower than in the west-side rainforests, but the range still holds heavy winter snowpack into midsummer. Expect fast-moving weather changes and afternoon thunderstorm risk typical of the Olympics.

bySeason.fall: Early October can still offer stable weather (NPS notes the Royal Basin hiking season runs into mid-October), but shortening days and new snow at the col make climbing increasingly marginal.
bySeason.spring: Heavy snowpack on the approach and technical terrain; not a recommended climbing season.
bySeason.summer: July through September is the driest, most snow-free window; the Clark-Johnson col and remnant glacier/snowfield below it usually clear substantially by mid-to-late July in an average year, but can hold snow into July after a heavy winter.
bySeason.winter: Not a recommended climbing objective; deep snow, avalanche hazard on the approach, and difficult trailhead access.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Olympics zone (winter/spring backcountry avalanche forecasts only; no summer alpine advisory)

climate.typical: Snow lingers on the upper mountain into July; the summit gully is often a steep snow chute requiring ice axe/crampons through late June–early July, transitioning to a dry, loose-rock scramble by August. First snow can return by late September–October.

bySeason.fall: Late September–October: first snow possible and shorter days, but still climbable in good weather.
bySeason.spring: Generally not climbed — Twin Lakes Road is usually still snowed-in or impassable.
bySeason.summer: August–September: typically dry loose talus/scree and rock scramble; the most reliable window.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — road access is closed by snow.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North / Mount Baker area (daily avalanche forecasts run roughly Thanksgiving–April; use the general Mountain Weather Forecast for summer trip planning).

climate.fall: Rain returns by October; conditions deteriorate quickly for scrambling.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack can linger into June on shaded gullies and the upper ridge.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable dry, snow-free window for the summit scramble.
climate.winter: Deep snow and frequent road/trail closures; not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Wet, temperate Olympic climate at the low trailhead (Staircase, ~825 ft) transitioning to alpine/subalpine conditions on Sawtooth Ridge; Flapjack Lakes and the upper mountain commonly hold snow into early summer.

bySeason.fall: Good conditions can persist into September/early October before snow returns; daylight shortens quickly for this long route.
bySeason.spring: Snow lingers in the approach gullies and the summit chockstone well into June — expect postholing and steep-snow travel.
bySeason.summer: Prime window is roughly late June/mid-July through September once the trail and rock have dried out — NPS gives late June-September as the general best season for the Flapjack Lakes Trail.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow with wind-slab/avalanche potential on the ridge; the access road can gate for weather in normal years independent of the current fire closure.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC publishes an Olympics avalanche forecast zone covering this range through the winter forecast season; outside that season use NWS point forecasts for the Olympics/Hood Canal area for trip planning.

climate.fall: Storms return by late September; conditions deteriorate quickly.
climate.spring: Heavy, wet snowpack persists into early summer; high avalanche danger on approach slopes.
climate.summer: Short, relatively dry climbing window (roughly Jul-Sep); the first week of August is statistically the driest period in the Pickets.
climate.winter: Cold, snowbound, and effectively inaccessible for this route.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate; most precipitation is driven off the Pacific and forced upward over the Cascade crest.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 — West Slopes North Cascades and Passes
