climate.winter: Road to Barlow Pass typically closed by snow; area not accessible
climate.typical: Low-elevation (~2,300-2,360 ft), forested, shaded valley-bottom setting on the west slope of the Cascades near Barlow Pass — consistent with the persistent moss growth noted in the route's own name and description.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone covering the Cascades of Snohomish County (near WAZ302 'Cascades of Snohomish and Northern King Counties')

climate.typical: Summer days on the exposed ridge are warm, sometimes over 80°F with little shade above Merritt Lake; snow and cornices can linger on the north-facing south-ridge catwalk into July.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly by late September/October; early snow possible above about 5,500 ft.
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered above Merritt Lake into June; active cornices on the south ridge — check NWAC before any spring attempt.
bySeason.summer: Best window (mid-July through September); generally dry and warm with occasional afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Becomes a ski/snowshoe approach toward Merritt and Lost Lakes; the summit ridge is avalanche/cornice terrain and not a standard winter scramble objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (winter/spring avalanche/cornice conditions); NWS Wenatchee Mountains zone for summer weather

climate.summer: Driest, most likely rock-dry season
climate.typical: Wet, maritime Cascade weather with a pronounced summer dry season
climate.forecastZone: Nearest official NWAC avalanche zone is Stevens Pass

climate.fall: Wet weather returns by October; road and brush conditions deteriorate.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the upper ridge and around the summit ponds into June; brush is wet and route-finding harder.
climate.summer: Jul-Sep is the most reliable dry window for a straightforward ascent.
climate.winter: Heavy snow makes this a popular snowshoe objective, but FR-62 is frequently unplowed/gated, and avalanche/route-finding hazard increases.
climate.typical: Wet, maritime-influenced Cascade climate with heavy winter precipitation and drier summers.
climate.forecastZone: NWS West Slopes North Central Cascades and Passes (zone WAZ568); Northwest Avalanche Center Stevens Pass zone for winter conditions

climate.fall: September and early October are excellent — cooler, quieter, stable high pressure common, and the huckleberry and heather colour on the basin below the pass is superb. Daylight shortens quickly against a 7-9 hour day, so start earlier than feels necessary, and the first autumn storms will put verglas on the chipped ledges without much warning.
climate.spring: Not the season for it. FR 2095 is typically snowbound through April and the Mountain Loop Highway is seasonally gated; wet heavy snow above Stujack Pass means real avalanche exposure on the steep basin and traverse. Anyone going in spring is doing a snow climb, not a scramble, and needs axe, crampons and avalanche judgement.
climate.summer: The prime window. Snow generally clears from the trail by early-to-mid July but lingers on the traverse above Stujack Pass — a late-July report found the trail clear with remaining snow above the pass expected to last another month. August is the most reliable for dry rock on the slab. Expect heat and full sun on the upper 4,000 ft, which is dry the whole way, and watch for afternoon convection over an exposed crest.
climate.winter: Effectively out of season. Road access is gated and unplowed, the approach becomes a long snow slog, and the exposed razorback crest with a permanent snowfield below it is serious winter mountaineering terrain in a zone known for wet heavy snow and high avalanche danger.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Pacific weather systems are forced upward by the Cascades and dump heavy precipitation on this side of the range; temperatures rarely fall below 0 F or rise above 80 F, and snow tends to be wet and heavy, which produces high avalanche danger in season. Cloud frequently sits on the ridge crest even when the valleys are clear, and the summit view that makes the peak famous is far from guaranteed.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC covers the west slopes of the North Cascades for avalanche and mountain weather; the Mountain Loop Highway / Darrington corridor falls in NWAC's west-slope North Cascades forecast area (West Slopes North). Confirm the exact zone on the NWAC map for your date, and pair it with an NWS point forecast for the summit coordinates.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with strong orographic precipitation off the Pacific — heavy winter snowfall builds and sustains the Queets Glacier despite the peak's modest elevation; summers are comparatively drier but still wet, with lingering snow/scree on shaded slopes into August.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues a dedicated 'Olympics' avalanche zone forecast during winter/spring for backcountry travel in this range

climate.typical: Rainier generates its own weather: Paradise held the world one-season snowfall record (1,122 in., winter 1971-72), and lenticular clouds capping the summit are a reliable sign of an approaching front. Sudden whiteouts and afternoon thunderstorms are common even on otherwise clear summer days.
climate.forecastZone: The Northwest Avalanche Center (NWAC) issues avalanche/weather forecasts only for terrain below 8,000 ft and only from late November to mid-April — there is no NWAC forecast covering the upper mountain during climbing season. Climbers rely on the park's own mountain-weather guidance and telemetry from Camp Muir/Paradise instead.

climate.fall: Early season storms; approach becomes increasingly committing
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack, high avalanche hazard on the approach glaciers
climate.summer: Best window (Jun-Jul) before the face becomes overly sun-affected
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible
climate.typical: Cold northwest-side ice; needs firm conditions.

bySeason.fall: Icy/broken, out of condition.
bySeason.spring: Approach snowbound, road closed.
bySeason.summer: Best window when ice is firm.
bySeason.winter: Extreme, rarely climbed.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Mount Rainier; NWAC Mount Rainier

NWAC issues avalanche/weather forecasts only for terrain below 8,000 ft and only from late November to mid-April — there is no NWAC forecast for the upper mountain in climbing season; rely on park mountain-weather guidance and Camp Schurman/White River telemetry instead.

climate.fall: Early snow returns; route rarely climbed
climate.spring: Prime window before full melt-out opens the bergschrund
climate.summer: Couloir becomes increasingly bare/icy and rockfall-prone as the season progresses
climate.winter: Cold but accessible via Paradise; rarely attempted
climate.typical: South-side spring couloir; warming-driven hazard.

bySeason.fall: Out of condition.
bySeason.spring: Prime firm snow early.
bySeason.summer: Melts out, rockfall.
bySeason.winter: Avalanche-prone, rarely climbed.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Mount Rainier; NWAC Mount Rainier

climate.typical: The north-side approach stays shaded and cold — expect overnight refreeze even in June — but the Carbon Glacier crossing and the ridge's lower rock bands warm quickly once the sun hits them, so climbers time river and glacier crossings for early morning.

bySeason.spring: Late-May trips can still run into full winter storms and deep new snow burying the route.
bySeason.summer: By July the ridge's rock bands are increasingly melted out and rockfall becomes the dominant hazard, overtaking the ice/weather risk more typical of May-June.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Seattle/Tacoma issues a Mount Rainier Recreational Forecast aimed at climbers (freezing levels, Rainier-specific point forecast); note that NWAC's backcountry avalanche forecast does not cover Rainier's climbing routes.

climate.fall: Increasing rain and shortening daylight narrow the practical window
climate.spring: Deep snowpack typically lingers in the upper basins and on the summit slopes into early summer
climate.summer: The most reliable window (Jul-Sep) but still unsettled — trip reports document rain and hail squalls even in early September
climate.winter: Heavy snow and storms make the multi-day approach and summit slopes impractical for most parties
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: wet, mild winters with heavy snow accumulation in the high interior, and a relatively short, more stable summer window. The standard scramble is typically driest and most snow-free from mid-July through September.

bySeason.summer: Best window (Jul-Sep) for the scree/talus scramble; expect long daylight but still-frequent Pacific frontal systems and afternoon cloud buildup typical of the Olympics.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and frequent storms make the approach trails themselves a serious undertaking; not a realistic season for this route.

climate.forecastZone: Olympic Mountains (NWAC forecasts this range in winter)

climate.fall: Lower Ruth Creek water levels ease the crossing, but brush is thick and days are shorter; early snow can return by October.
climate.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack with elevated avalanche hazard on the approach slopes and gullies; wet-slide risk grows through the day as the sun warms south-facing terrain.
climate.summer: The primary climbing window (Jun-Sep); snow patches persist into July in shaded gullies, and afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
climate.winter: Rarely climbed; heavy snowfall, avalanche danger, and a highly corniced summit ridge make it a serious, treacherous winter objective.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate — wet, snowy winters and drier but changeable summers; the Cascade crest generates its own fast-moving weather, so forecasts can shift quickly.

bySeason.fall: Often the most stable, driest window with lower creek levels, but shorter daylight and possible early-season snow by October.
bySeason.spring: Firm morning snow can make a snow-line ascent (Wall Street Couloir/Northwest Glacier to the SE ridge) attractive, but wet-slide avalanche hazard and cornices rise quickly through the day.
bySeason.summer: Prime rock-route season mid-July through September once the gullies bare out; Ruth Creek runs highest with snowmelt in June, easing later in summer.
bySeason.winter: Deep snowpack and high avalanche hazard; access road often snowed-in.

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC zone for this peak; use the NWAC Mt. Baker Zone avalanche forecast (spring snow routes) and the NWS Bellingham/North Cascades point forecast for current conditions.

climate.typical: Wet, maritime snowpack with frequent cloud and rain on the approach even in summer; the chimneys and upper glaciers commonly hold snow into July
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker zone
NWAC Mt. Baker zone

climate.summer: Best window
climate.typical: Wet maritime Cascade weather
climate.forecastZone: NWAC/NWS Mt. Baker zone

climate.fall: Early snow can return by late September-October and days shorten quickly, closing the window.
climate.spring: Approach road and trail are typically snow-covered/washed out; not a practical season for this route.
climate.summer: July-September brings the most consistent weather and driest approach brush, though afternoon thunderstorms and cloud-in are still common.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; access via Depot Creek Road and the border crossing is effectively unavailable.
climate.typical: Short climbing season with snowpack often lingering into July on the upper mountain. North Cascades weather here is changeable — fast-moving frontal systems, wind, and even summer snow showers are possible at this elevation so close to the crest.
climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC zone covers this far-northern, cross-border area; use the NPS North Cascades backcountry weather/trip-planning guidance for the US side and Environment Canada's Fraser Valley/North Shore mountain forecast for the BC approach.

climate.typical: Weather on the upper mountain can deteriorate rapidly with little warning — wind, whiteout cloud, and temperature drops are common even on days that start clear at the trailhead. There are no glaciers on the current south-side route, but permanent snowfields with icy, cracked surfaces persist into summer on the upper slopes.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes South zone covers Mount St. Helens weather and avalanche forecasting.

climate.typical: Winter and spring ascents mean full alpine conditions on the upper mountain — high wind, blowing snow, and whiteout cloud are common even when Cougar and the lowlands are clear. Avalanche and cornice hazard are directly tied to recent snowfall and wind loading.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes South zone covers Mount St. Helens avalanche and mountain weather forecasts.

climate.fall: Good conditions into September/October with the driest, most stable weather, shortening daylight for the long approach.
climate.spring: Trailhead and lower valley are often snow-free, but the route above ~4,000-5,000 ft (Marmot Lake and the summit amphitheater) typically still holds significant snowpack.
climate.summer: Best climbing window; snow retreats from the upper mountain by roughly July, though patches can linger into early July.
climate.winter: Heavy snow, avalanche hazard, and difficult access; not a standard-season objective.
climate.typical: Wet, snow-heavy winters and cool, damp shoulder seasons typical of the interior Olympics; only a short mid-to-late-summer window offers reliably dry, snow-free scrambling.

bySeason.fall: Generally stable but days shorten quickly and early snow can return to the basin by October
bySeason.spring: High avalanche and wet-slide hazard on the upper mountain; approach-trail creek crossings run high and cold
bySeason.summer: Prime window is roughly mid/late July through September; cornices and steep snow can still guard the summit ridge into late June
bySeason.winter: Deep snowpack typically makes both the access road and trail impractical

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Olympics zone (seasonal avalanche forecasts); this interior summit is above the range's typical observation network, so use forecast trends plus on-the-ground judgment rather than route-specific advisories.

climate.typical: A wet, brushy western Cascades foothill peak — at only 5,307 ft the trailhead and lower approach see rain more than snow much of the year, but the shaded summit gully and upper basin can hold snow and ice into June and refill with the season's first storms in October-November.

bySeason.fall: Good conditions typically hold into October until the rains return; shorter daylight means an earlier start.
bySeason.spring: Lingering snow in the gully and upper basin commonly persists into June; underlying rock/mud can be wet and slick where snow has thinned.
bySeason.summer: The reliable window (roughly July-September): gully is snow-free but still loose and often muddy/slick in the 4th class section; brush on the lower approach is fully leafed out.
bySeason.winter: A locally popular low-elevation snow climb; expect to boot-pack or kick steps up the summit gully and to rope up for it, plus manage cornice and avalanche hazard on the upper mountain — check the NWAC Stevens Pass forecast beforehand.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC — Stevens Pass zone (relevant for winter/spring ascents when the summit gully and approach are snow-covered).

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: wet, heavy-snow winters and drier, warmer summers; orographic lift off the Pacific creates rapid weather changes on the Cascade crest.

bySeason.fall: Climbable into September/early October with shorter days and rising chance of early-season snow late in the season.
bySeason.spring: Snow lingers on north-facing approach slopes and in Bumblebee Basin well into June.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (late July-September); warm days with real afternoon thunderstorm risk, especially in August.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche hazard effectively close off the route.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (most relevant for assessing shoulder-season snow on the approach)

climate.fall: Increasing rain and shortening stable-weather windows
climate.spring: Wet, with elevated avalanche and weak-snow-bridge hazard on the Blue Glacier and White Glacier
climate.summer: Driest, most stable window for glacier travel, roughly July-September
climate.winter: Very heavy rain/snow at the trailhead and deep snow up high; route not recommended, and road washouts are more common
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: heavy winter snowfall, persistent snowpack into July on the Bailey Range crest and glaciers, and generally wet, cloudy conditions even in summer. The Hoh side of the approach is one of the wettest places in the Lower 48; expect rain gear to be essential regardless of forecast.

bySeason.fall: Snowfree by September/October but shortening daylight and increasing storm frequency narrow the window quickly; first snows can arrive by early October.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack and high avalanche danger on approach slopes; route generally not attempted.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the practical climbing window; late July into August typically offers the best balance of snow-bridge coverage on the glacier and manageable rock/scree lower down, though afternoon cloud, fog, or convective showers are still common.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — heavy snow, avalanche hazard, and extremely difficult access.

climate.forecastZone: Olympic Mountains west-slope / Hoh Rainforest zone (NWS Seattle forecast area)

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate — wetter winters, drier/more stable summers July–September, occasional afternoon thunderstorms.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (winter-only avalanche forecasts); check NPS Boston Basin climbing-conditions blog for summer beta.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet, heavy-snow winters and generally drier, more stable summers. July–September brings the most consistent weather, though afternoon thunderstorms and sudden fronts still occur.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (avalanche forecasts run mid-November through mid-April only; for summer conditions check the NPS 'Climbing Conditions – Boston Basin Area' blog and NWS zone WAZ567)

climate.typical: The southeastern Olympics sit in the rain shadow of the higher western peaks but still see heavy orographic precipitation off Hood Canal and Puget Sound; conditions can change quickly on the exposed upper mountain.

bySeason.fall: Good scrambling conditions often persist into early-mid October, but early snow can arrive on the upper ridge with little warning.
bySeason.spring: Snow typically still covers the gullies, saddle, and upper meadows into May/June, turning the scramble into a steep snow climb — ice axe (and often crampons) required; avalanche hazard should be assessed via NWAC before travel.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the prime dry-scramble window, but the upper mountain has little shade and days can be hot and muggy; afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
bySeason.winter: Not a standard winter objective — deep snow, avalanche terrain in the gullies, and an unplowed/gated access road make it a serious undertaking outside the summer/fall window.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "Olympics" zone (Northwest Avalanche Center) for winter/spring snow conditions.

climate.fall: Weather turns wetter and more unsettled into October, and shorter days tighten the margin for the long approach.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the approach and ridge, especially beyond Chicago Camp; an ice axe is often needed.
climate.summer: July-September is the recommended climbing season with the most reliably snow-free travel.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; deep snow and avalanche-prone approach terrain.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: wet, mild winters with heavy snow accumulation at elevation, and drier, more stable summers. July through September gives the most reliable weather window for the climb; snow can persist on upper north- and shaded slopes into July.

bySeason.fall: Shortening days and increasing odds of early-season storms; a good but narrowing window through September.
bySeason.spring: Trail is passable but upper approach and summit slopes typically still hold significant snow; river fords run higher with snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best window for the climb; generally the clearest and driest stretch, though still subject to Pacific frontal systems passing through.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snowfall and avalanche-prone approach slopes; the access road is often affected by washouts/closures. Effectively a winter mountaineering objective, not a scramble, during this season.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Olympic Peninsula / NWAC does not forecast this zone directly — check NPS Olympic wilderness trail-conditions updates and general Olympic Peninsula NWS forecasts.

climate.typical: A short alpine window bookended by SR 20's seasonal closure: realistically climbable only roughly April/May through October/November, with the best rock conditions from late July through September.

bySeason.fall: September is the recommended month — settled weather, cooler temps, and the surrounding larches turning color — but SR 20 can close abruptly with early-season snow, so don't wait too late.
bySeason.spring: SR 20 typically reopens in April; the approach gully and talus are usually still snow-covered well into June, requiring crampons/axe and making travel slower and more hazardous (steep, dicey traverses reported even in mid-June).
bySeason.summer: Warmest and driest window, but a snow patch near the summit can persist into early July and make the crux step-across wet; afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible — SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated and closed, typically from late November or early December into April or early May.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC's Washington Pass weather station (nwac.us) is the most relevant real-time data point; check NWAC's mountain weather forecast and NWS zone forecasts for the East Slopes of the North Cascades for planning.

climate.fall: Shortening days and early snow can return quickly at this latitude and elevation.
climate.spring: Deep snowpack; approach road and lower trail often still snow-covered or brushed-in.
climate.summer: The realistic climbing window; still expect lingering snow and possible cornices on the ridge in early summer.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; heavy snow and avalanche terrain with no maintained access.
climate.typical: Wet, snowy North Cascades maritime climate; heavy winter snowpack lingers on north-facing slopes into July, giving a short July-September climbing window
climate.forecastZone: No NWAC zone covers this area directly — use a NOAA point forecast for the Marblemount/Cascade River area and check recent Snowking/Buckindy trip reports for current snow line

climate.fall: Early snow can arrive by mid-to-late September at this elevation, and shortening days plus the boat/shuttle schedule compress the usable window.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snow into June keeps the off-trail gullies avalanche-prone and makes the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail hard to follow.
climate.summer: Late July through September offers the most reliable dry, snow-free scrambling window (as in the documented September 2023 ascent).
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible — Stehekin itself is snowed in and boat/floatplane service is reduced; no winter ascents are documented.
climate.typical: Dry, warm summer days at elevation with cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are possible July-August. North-facing terrain below the crux holds snow later into summer than typical south-facing Cascades approaches.

bySeason.fall: A narrow window in early-to-mid September is possible before fall snow returns; days shorten quickly and access logistics (ferry schedule) get tighter.
bySeason.spring: Generally not viable — snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the crux terrain well into early summer.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the best window, though early-summer parties report lingering snow in the 5,000 ft slab gully and upper gullies into July.
bySeason.winter: Not a recognized route — roadless Stehekin access, avalanche exposure on the approach, and the technical crux make a winter ascent impractical for typical parties.

climate.forecastZone: Approximately NWS Zone WAZ522, "Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest" (forecast.weather.gov)

climate.fall: September-early October often gives stable, cool, dry conditions before winter gating.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May; the shaded gully holds snow/ice well into early summer.
climate.summer: June-September is the main season, though the gully can still carry snow early on.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the peak is effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate: heavy, wet winter snowpack and drier, warmer continental summers.
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass has its own NWAC weather station (5,477 ft); the area falls within NWAC's East Slopes avalanche forecasting and the NWS 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest' zone (WAZ522)

climate.fall: Good climbing into September before fall rains
climate.spring: Often too wet, with lingering snow near 5,000 ft and possible road gate closures
climate.summer: Warm and dry — the primary season
climate.winter: Access roads gated; not a winter objective
climate.typical: Prime climbing window is July-September
climate.forecastZone: Southern WA Cascades / Mt. Adams region

climate.fall: The route is rarely climbed in fall due to lack of consolidated snow/ice.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May, which is also the prime climbing window; avalanche and cornice hazard remain high in this period.
climate.summer: By June-July the couloir has usually melted out into a looser mixed/rock scramble with more rockfall.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the couloir is inaccessible from the highway side.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate with heavy, wet winter/spring snowpack; the pass corridor is among the highest-avalanche-frequency stretches of highway in the US.
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass has its own NWAC weather station (5,477 ft); the area falls within NWAC's East Slopes avalanche forecasting and the NWS 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest' zone (WAZ522) - check the current avalanche/mountain weather forecast before a spring ascent

climate.fall: September-early October often gives stable, cool, dry conditions before winter gating.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May; the east side can still hold snow in the approach gully.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable rock season.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the peak is effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate: heavy, wet winter snowpack and drier, warmer continental summers.

climate.fall: September-early October often gives stable, cool, dry conditions before winter gating.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May; snow can linger into June.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable rock season.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the peak is effectively inaccessible.

climate.fall: Shortening daylight and increasing storm frequency; possible narrow late-season window
climate.spring: Heavy, wet snowpack; high avalanche hazard, not a climbing season for this route
climate.summer: The only realistic climbing window; couloir snow/ice conditions vary year to year
climate.winter: Not climbed — deep wet snow and avalanche hazard
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the North Cascades: heavy Pacific precipitation and very deep winter snowpack, with a short practical window for the route roughly mid-July through September. Even in summer, the shaded approach gully and Price Glacier can hold snow/ice later than nearby lower terrain.

bySeason.fall: Water levels in Ruth Creek and the Nooksack River drop, easing the fords, but the route itself becomes increasingly icy and less climbable as September ends.
bySeason.spring: Approach fords are typically at their highest and most dangerous from spring snowmelt; the tower itself is not a realistic spring rock objective.
bySeason.summer: The only practical climbing window; still expect possible afternoon convective showers and lingering snow/ice in the approach gully into July.
bySeason.winter: Effectively unclimbable as a rock route — heavy snowpack and avalanche terrain dominate the approach.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mount Baker zone (useful for approach snow/avalanche conditions in the shoulder season)

climate.fall: Shortening daylight, increasing storms; narrow late-season window at best
climate.spring: Heavy, wet snowpack; not a climbing season for this route
climate.summer: The only realistic window; glacier icefall and face conditions vary year to year
climate.winter: Not climbed
climate.typical: South-facing aspect means earlier snow melt and rockfall hazard. Morning may have residual frost; afternoon heat can weaken snow/ice bonds and accelerate rockfall.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker zone; point forecasts available via mountain-forecast.com (Mount Shuksan)

climate.typical: East of the Cascade Crest in a strong rain shadow - drier, sunnier, and with bigger day-to-night temperature swings than west-side North Cascades routes.

bySeason.fall: Cool, often stable weather through September; first snow can arrive by early-to-mid October
bySeason.spring: Deep snowpack lingers in the basin and bowls into June; the trail may still hold snow patches near Gardner Meadows
bySeason.summer: Warm and mostly dry; July-August is peak season, though afternoon thunderstorms can build over the Cascade Crest
bySeason.winter: Not a realistic season without full winter mountaineering gear - access roads and the approach are typically snowed in

climate.forecastZone: NWAC's East Slopes North zone covers the Washington Pass/Methow area (useful for spring snow conditions in the approach basins); NWS Spokane forecast zone for local weather

climate.typical: Wet, heavy-snowpack North Cascades winters give way to a short summer climbing window; the Lyman Lakes/Cloudy Pass basin commonly holds snow into July, and the Spider Gap notch can carry a firm snowfield into August. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August with fast-moving weather near the crest.

bySeason.fall: Early fall (September) often brings the most snow-free talus and the most stable weather before autumn storms return, but daylight shortens quickly.
bySeason.summer: July through September is the only realistic window; even then expect residual snow patches above Lyman Lakes and at Spider Gap into early-to-mid August.

climate.forecastZone: Central Washington Cascades (use NWS Spokane zone forecasts for Chelan County high terrain); this is non-ski, non-glaciated terrain not covered by NWAC avalanche forecasts.

climate.typical: Cool, wet, and glacier-influenced even in mid-summer; the Chilliwack/Picket high country sits directly against the Cascade crest and catches heavy precipitation, with fast-moving fog and afternoon cloud buildup common even on otherwise clear days.

bySeason.fall: Snow can return to the high peaks by late September, closing the technical route for the year; approach creek/waterfall flows drop and become easier as summer progresses.
bySeason.spring: Generally not viable; high snow load on the approach and glacier, and Depot Creek Falls runs at its most dangerous with peak snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Jul-Sep is the only realistic climbing window; long daylight hours but real potential for afternoon rain, thunderstorms, and fog even during a forecast "good weather" stretch.
bySeason.winter: Not a viable season — heavy snowpack, avalanche-prone approach terrain, and an unmaintained trail make the route effectively inaccessible.

climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades) for general mountain weather; NWAC's avalanche and mountain-weather forecasts only run roughly November-April and do not cover this summer-only climbing season.

climate.fall: Good climbing into September before fall rains
climate.spring: Often too wet, with lingering snow near 5,000 ft and possible road gate closures
climate.summer: Warm and dry — the primary season
climate.winter: Access roads gated; not a winter objective
climate.typical: Prime climbing window is July-September

climate.fall: September-early October often gives stable, cool, dry conditions before winter gating.
climate.spring: SR-20 typically reopens late April-May; snow can linger into June on shaded ledges.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable rock season; the west-facing rock can get hot in the afternoon.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed (roughly December-April/May); the peak is effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate: heavy, wet winter snowpack and drier, warmer continental summers.
climate.forecastZone: Washington Pass has its own NWAC weather station (5,477 ft); the area falls within NWAC's East Slopes avalanche forecasting and the NWS 'Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest' zone (WAZ522)

climate.fall: Good climbing into September before fall rains
climate.spring: Often too wet, with lingering snow near 5,000 ft and possible road gate closures
climate.summer: Warm and dry — the primary season
climate.winter: Access roads gated; not a winter objective
climate.typical: Prime climbing window is July-September
climate.forecastZone: Southern WA Cascades / Mt. Adams region

climate.typical: A short alpine summer window bracketed by the access road's own snow closure — Harts Pass Road is typically snowed in from late October to early July.

bySeason.fall: Cools quickly after mid-September; first snow can close the road again by October.
bySeason.spring: Road closed by snow into June/early July most years; heavy snowfields persist on the approach and route.
bySeason.summer: Best window, mid-July through September; afternoon thunderstorms are common in this east-of-the-crest, continental-influenced part of the North Cascades.
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible — road gated and snowed in, no maintained winter access.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes North zone (avalanche forecasters are on duty roughly mid-November to mid-April; use NWS point forecasts for summer conditions).

climate.fall: Clear, cooler, often stable weather into September; shorter daylight, and the highway can begin closing as early as late fall.
climate.spring: Approach trail and the 6,500 ft bench can hold lingering snow into June; the route itself is often still wet or snow-patched early season.
climate.summer: Prime climbing season (Jul-Aug): generally warm and dry with afternoon thunderstorm potential.
climate.winter: SR 20 is gated closed (roughly Dec-Apr); the peak is inaccessible by vehicle.
climate.typical: High alpine granite-spire climate: warm, mostly dry summers with afternoon thunderstorm risk typical of the East Cascades, and cold, snowy winters that close SR 20 entirely.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Okanogan County/East Slopes Washington Cascades zone; NWAC's East Slopes Cascades avalanche zone covers this area but only issues forecasts in winter/spring, not during the summer rock season

climate.fall: Clear, cooler, often stable weather into September; shorter daylight, and the highway can begin closing as early as late fall.
climate.spring: Approach trail and the 6,500 ft bench can hold lingering snow into June; lower pitches are often wet early season.
climate.summer: Prime climbing season (Jul-Aug): generally warm and dry with afternoon thunderstorm potential.
climate.winter: SR 20 is gated closed (roughly Dec-Apr); the peak is inaccessible by vehicle.
climate.typical: High alpine granite-spire climate: warm, mostly dry summers with afternoon thunderstorm risk typical of the East Cascades, and cold, snowy winters that close SR 20 entirely.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Okanogan County/East Slopes Washington Cascades zone; NWAC's East Slopes Cascades avalanche zone covers this area but only issues forecasts in winter/spring, not during the summer rock season

climate.fall: September offers crisp, stable weather; less likely for afternoon convection. Shorter days; sunrise near 6:30 AM, sunset near 7:00 PM.
climate.spring: Snow likely on approaches and lower pitches through May; corn snow conditions develop in late April-May; cooler and shorter days.
climate.summer: Stable weather generally July-August; mornings clear, afternoon thunderstorms possible. Daytime highs 50-65°F; nights near freezing. Sunrise near 4:45 AM, sunset near 8:45 PM.
climate.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche danger; Highway 20 often closed east of pass; not typically climbed.
climate.typical: Alpine environment with rapid weather changes. Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer; afternoon winds increase. Temperature variability from freezing at dawn to 50-60°F on south aspects at midday.
climate.forecastZone: National Weather Service Eastern Washington (Okanogan County)

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows and increasing storm frequency by late September
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists into early summer; access trails/roads may still be snow-covered
climate.summer: Primary climbing season; still expect residual snow/glacier travel well into July
climate.winter: Deep snowpack, avalanche terrain, and essentially inaccessible without ski/snowshoe mountaineering skills
climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters and springs with a short, relatively dry climbing window in summer
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades); NWAC West Slopes North avalanche zone for shoulder-season snow conditions

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows, increasing storm frequency by late September
climate.spring: Deep snowpack persists into early summer on approach trails and passes
climate.summer: Primary season; glacier/snow conditions on route still evolve through July as the season progresses
climate.winter: Heavy snowpack and avalanche terrain make this essentially a ski-mountaineering-only proposition
climate.typical: Maritime alpine climate typical of the North Cascades: heavy snowpack lingers into July, with frequent fog, low cloud, and the possibility of afternoon thunderstorms even in the prime summer window. Weather in the Pickets specifically is known for being unusually fickle and hard to forecast precisely.

bySeason.fall: Early-season snow can arrive by late September, shortening the practical window.
bySeason.spring: Approach trails and creek crossings are typically unsafe/impassable due to high water and lingering snow into June.
bySeason.summer: Late July through August is the most reliable window for the technical sections to be in reasonable condition, though bugs in Luna Cirque peak in July.
bySeason.winter: Not a viable season — approach roads and trails are snowed in and avalanche hazard is extreme.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC does not forecast the Pickets directly; use the Washington Pass/North Cascades Highway zone and Mount Baker-area forecasts as the nearest proxies, and cross-check NPS trip-report/ranger updates.

climate.typical: Typical west-slope Cascades maritime weather: wet, mild winters with the rain-snow line frequently at or above this summit's 4,258 ft, and drier but still changeable summers. Fog and low cloud are common in the Skykomish valley, especially fall through winter, which makes off-trail routefinding on the ridge harder.

bySeason.fall: Cooler and often drier air, but shorter days and increasing rain; moss-covered rock on the ridge gets slick.
bySeason.spring: Snow often lingers on the upper ridge into May; isothermal, rotten snow over the boulder field can hide holes and is the main spring hazard.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the driest window but slide alder and salmonberry are at their thickest, making the off-trail section slow and scratchy.
bySeason.winter: Rain up to roughly 4,000 ft is common; when snow does accumulate it buries the brush and speeds travel, but requires snowshoes, winter navigation skill in potential whiteout, and awareness of wind-loading near the cliff band.

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated avalanche/weather forecast zone covers this sub-4,300' summit specifically; NWAC's Stevens Pass zone forecast is the nearest useful reference for general winter conditions, not a precise substitute.

climate.typical: Cool mornings warming quickly once the sun hits the south-facing gully; sudden afternoon thunderstorms and gusty wind are common on this exposed ridge in summer.

bySeason.fall: Often uncrowded and dry into September and early October, until Stevens Canyon Road closes for the season; first snow can arrive by October.
bySeason.spring: Trail and summit gully are typically still snow-covered into June, and Stevens Canyon Road itself may not be open yet.
bySeason.summer: Prime season, roughly July through September; expect the trail to be snow-free by mid-to-late July in an average year, though the gully can hold snow patches longer. Watch for typical Cascades afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Road closed and gated; the peak is essentially inaccessible without a long snow approach and avalanche skills.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mount Rainier / West Slopes South zone — mainly relevant for late-spring/early-season snow on the approach; NWAC forecasting is intermittent through the summer climbing season.

climate.typical: Cool, changeable subalpine weather. The Tatoosh Range catches Mount Rainier's heavy winter snowpack (often well over 10 ft), which can linger on the saddle approach into July. Summers are mild (50s-70s F) with a strong diurnal pattern - clear mornings, building cumulus, and a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms and lightning by early-to-mid afternoon in July and August.

bySeason.fall: Good, quieter conditions into September and early October until the road closes for winter.
bySeason.spring: Trail tread and the saddle boot path are often still snow-covered into June.
bySeason.summer: Prime season; peak wildflower bloom late July-August; afternoon thunderstorm risk is highest in this window.
bySeason.winter: Buried in deep snow; Stevens Canyon Road is closed, so winter/spring access requires a much longer approach on snowshoes from Paradise or Narada Falls.

climate.forecastZone: NWS Paradise, WA point forecast; NWAC's Mount Rainier zone covers the mountain's glaciers and is most relevant for winter avalanche conditions rather than this summer scramble.

climate.typical: South-side Rainier weather is driven by Pacific frontal systems, with rapid afternoon cloud buildup and thunderstorm potential in summer; the connecting chutes between Success and Kautz Cleavers see meaningful rock and icefall as daily freeze-thaw cycles let go.

bySeason.fall: September: still climbable but increasingly cold, with an early season snowpack sometimes returning by late month; upper crevasse bridges near the Kautz Cleaver junction begin thinning.
bySeason.spring: Mid-May-June: the cleaver is still largely snow-covered, which is actually the preferred condition — it buries the loose talus/scree and speeds travel, though cornice and wind-slab hazard exists high on the connecting chutes.
bySeason.summer: July-August: snow retreats to expose steep, unstable, unconsolidated scree and choss on the Divide and lower cleaver; heat and biting insects at lower elevations (Indian Henry's/Mirror Lakes) become the main nuisance on the approach.
bySeason.winter: Not a practical winter objective — access alone (unplowed/unmaintained approach trail, avalanche terrain) makes winter ascents very rare.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues forecasts only up to about 8,000 ft and only from late November-mid April; there is no formal avalanche forecast covering this route's elevation, so climbers must assess snow and rockfall conditions themselves on the upper cleaver.

climate.fall: Conditions deteriorate quickly after early-mid September — a late-September attempt found this route complicated by early-season ice and snow.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack on approach and route through May-June; Thunder Creek runs high with snowmelt.
climate.summer: Best climbing window, roughly July-September, once Lucky Ridge and the glacier approach have melted out; afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
climate.winter: Full winter conditions with avalanche hazard, deep-snow approach, and short daylight; occasional winter ascents are documented (e.g. a February trip requiring skis and a packraft creek crossing).
climate.typical: Marine-influenced Cascade alpine climate: heavy winter snowpack lingers on the Borealis Glacier into July; summer days can still bring fast-moving Pacific frontal systems with rain and whiteout above treeline, and multiple trip reports specifically note cloud/fog socking in the summit on otherwise clear days.

bySeason.fall: By September the Borealis Glacier is largely bare and thin-bridged over its crevasses; a documented late-Sept attempt found the route iced up and the standard col unreachable.
bySeason.spring: Deep, avalanche-prone snowpack on the approach slopes; outside NWAC's forecast season after mid-April, so climbers are on their own for hazard assessment.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Aug); watch for afternoon thunderstorms and fast-forming fog on the glacier.
bySeason.winter: Rarely climbed; a Feb. 2022 winter ascent required skis, crampons, and a packraft to cross Thunder Creek where the trail bridge was out.

climate.forecastZone: NWS/NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (WAZ567). NWAC's daily avalanche forecast for this zone only runs mid-November to mid-April, outside the normal climbing season.

climate.fall: Deteriorates quickly after early-mid September — a late-September attempt found the ridge iced ('bullet ice') and considerably harder than its summer rating.
climate.spring: Likely fully snow/ice covered and not a viable rock objective.
climate.summer: Primary window, roughly July-early September, before route conditions deteriorate.
climate.winter: Not a documented winter rock objective on this ridge.
climate.typical: Same marine-influenced alpine climate as the rest of the Primus massif — wet winters, lingering snow into July, and a real chance of fast-moving cloud/fog on summit day.
climate.forecastZone: NWS/NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (WAZ567); avalanche forecasts only run mid-Nov to mid-Apr, outside climbing season.

climate.typical: Wet, maritime west-slope Cascades climate with frequent rain and low cloud; snow can linger in the Rainy Lake basin and on the summit ridge into July in a heavy-snow year.

bySeason.fall: Good, cooler weather through September into early October; watch for early-season snow at elevation and shortening daylight.
bySeason.spring: Trail and creek crossings plus the boot path above Rainy Lake are commonly snow-covered into June; route-finding landmarks can be buried — carry a GPS track or map/compass.
bySeason.summer: Best conditions; brush is out and the ridge above Rainy Lake is typically snow-free by mid-to-late July.
bySeason.winter: Feasible as a snowshoe/snow-climb objective for experienced, avalanche-trained parties (offered as a Mountaineers winter scramble), but FR 56 access and avalanche hazard on the ridge and basin above Rainy Lake are limiting factors.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC — Snoqualmie Pass zone (for winter/spring snow conditions)

climate.typical: Marine-influenced Cascade alpine climate with a heavy, wet snowpack that persists on the Eldorado/Inspiration/North Klawatti glaciers well into summer; expect afternoon cloud buildup and possible thunderstorms even on otherwise clear forecasts.

bySeason.fall: By September, glaciers on this route become notably more melted-out and crevassed, with thin, unreliable snow bridges — one September party described probing every step with a whippet due to bridges that would poke through when stepped on.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (July-August) with the most reliable snow bridges over crevasses on the glacier crossings.

climate.forecastZone: NWS/NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (WAZ567); NWAC's avalanche forecast for this zone only runs mid-November through mid-April.

climate.typical: Sunny south-facing granite; afternoon thunderstorms common in summer.

bySeason.fall: Crisp and dry, larches turning; excellent climbing.
bySeason.spring: Snowbound; long snowy approach.
bySeason.summer: Prime season; warm dry granite, afternoon storm risk.
bySeason.winter: Full winter approach; rarely climbed as rock.

climate.forecastZone: Washington Central Cascades (Alpine Lakes / Enchantments)

climate.typical: Sunny south-facing granite; afternoon thunderstorms common in summer.

bySeason.fall: Crisp and dry, larches turning; excellent climbing.
bySeason.spring: Snowbound; long snowy approach.
bySeason.summer: Prime season; warm dry granite, afternoon storm risk.
bySeason.winter: Full winter approach; rarely climbed as rock.

climate.forecastZone: Washington Central Cascades (Alpine Lakes / Enchantments)

climate.typical: North Cascades crest weather: can be sunny and dry in July-August but afternoon thunderstorms build quickly on the exposed high ridges; snow is possible at 8,600 ft in any month. Strong west winds are common on the summit ridge.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in the basins by late September-early October; cold nights and early snow risk increase quickly after mid-September.
bySeason.summer: Best window; snow can linger on north-facing terrain and high passes into early July. Wildflower meadows and larch-lined basins along the Eureka/Berk Creek approaches.
bySeason.winter: Rarely climbed; ski/snowmobile approach via the Billy Goat trailhead (~40 mile round trip) or Monument Creek (avalanche exposure near Monument Creek and Pistol Pass). A documented ascent on Feb 27-28, 2021 recorded 7°F and heavy wind on the summit.

climate.forecastZone: NWS North Cascades/Okanogan zone forecast; check NWAC for avalanche advisories if attempting outside summer.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with strong orographic lift off the Pacific: expect frequent cloud/rain outside the July–September window, heavy wet snowfall in winter, and a real chance of building afternoon thunderstorms even during the summer climbing season.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' (Baker/Skagit) zone for winter/shoulder-season snowpack and avalanche information — note NWAC issues avalanche forecasts primarily in the winter/spring season, not during the July–September climbing window.

climate.fall: Prime season; larch turn gold in late September–early October, though early snow is possible by then
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the trail and in the ascent gully into May–June; early starts and traction gear are common
climate.summer: Warm and mostly dry with real afternoon thunderstorm risk; mosquitoes can be heavy near Libby Lake and the old cabin
climate.winter: Heavy snow typically renders the approach road and trail impassable to most parties from roughly November through May
climate.typical: Dry, sunny East-Cascades continental climate — warm summers, cold snowy winters, and generally less precipitation than the west-side Cascades
climate.forecastZone: Not covered by NWAC's avalanche forecast zones (central/east-Cascades interior, incl. the Methow Valley, falls outside NWAC's zone coverage)

climate.typical: Typical Central Cascades crest weather: wet, snowy winters and springs give way to a dry-ish summer window. Snow can linger in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper west slope into early-to-mid July in an average year.

bySeason.fall: Good, often driest and most stable scrambling window into September and early October; days shorten fast and first snow can arrive by late October.
bySeason.spring: Basin and upper mountain typically still snow-covered; this becomes a snowshoe/ski-touring approach to Red Pass rather than a rock scramble.
bySeason.summer: Prime season once the upper slope clears, usually by mid-to-late July; watch for afternoon thunderstorms building over the crest in July/August.
bySeason.winter: Not a scrambling objective — deep snow, avalanche terrain in the basin, and no maintained winter access to the summit rock.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone for winter/spring snow conditions; NWS point forecast for the Alpine Lakes Wilderness/Snoqualmie Pass area for summer scrambling weather.

climate.fall: September-early October excellent; crisp mornings, stable systems more frequent; larch meadows in peak color; October above 8,000 feet increasingly cold, possible early snow
climate.spring: May conditions variable with lingering snow patches below 8,000 feet; stable weather becoming more common late May
climate.summer: July-August most stable with long daylight hours; afternoon thunderstorms common; warm days (60-70F at summit), freezing nights
climate.winter: November-April snow-covered with avalanche hazard and extreme cold; generally not climbed during winter
climate.typical: Variable mountain weather with potential for rapid changes. Frequent exposure to lightning in upper terrain.
climate.forecastZone: Mount Remmel area served by National Weather Service forecast for northern Washington Cascades and Mountain Forecast weather predictions

climate.fall: Clear, cool, and stable through September, with the first snowfall of the season typically closing out access in October.
climate.spring: Snow lingers into June on the approach trails; higher terrain often not clear until late June/July.
climate.summer: Warm, dry days with cool nights; afternoon thunderstorm risk on exposed ridges and the summit.
climate.winter: Cold, snowbound, and largely inaccessible; snow falls October-May across the wilderness.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny summers with occasional afternoon thunderstorms; noticeably drier and warmer than the west-side Cascades due to the rain shadow.
climate.forecastZone: East-slope North Cascades / Pasayten Wilderness (rain-shadow, continental-influenced)

climate.summer: Summer is the working window. Early in the season the glaciers on the approach are well covered with snow; as the summer goes on they show more bare ice, the Le Conte Glacier above all, so late-season parties may meet hard ice there.
climate.typical: The approach follows the Cascade crest, which divides the wetter, cloudier west side from the drier, warmer east side; the ridge itself lies on the east side. Storms can bring days of rain and wind even in summer, so allow a spare day for weather.
climate.forecastZone: Not covered by NWAC avalanche forecasts during the summer climbing season; its daily forecasts end in spring.

climate.typical: East-Cascades rain-shadow climate: dry, sunny, often hot summers with little to no shade on the lower switchbacks, and cold, snowy winters. Afternoon thunderstorms build regularly in July-August.

bySeason.fall: Comfortable hiking temperatures and golden larches along the ridge; days shorten quickly and the first snow can arrive by mid-to-late October.
bySeason.spring: Lower south-facing switchbacks can be snow-free by late June in light-snow years, but expect lingering snow and potential postholing above the Rock Lake saddle and on the summit ridge into early July.
bySeason.summer: Hot and dry on the exposed lower trail with little to no shade; carry more water than you think, as there are no reliable sources. Afternoon thunderstorms build on most days in July-August.
bySeason.winter: Snowbound and avalanche-prone terrain; not a winter hiking objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone for general mountain weather/avalanche context (winter/spring); no dedicated NWAC summer product — check Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts for trail conditions and fire restrictions in summer.

climate.typical: Maritime alpine climate; the glacier is more snow-covered and forgiving early summer, more open and icy by early fall
climate.forecastZone: Check the NPS Boston Basin climbing-conditions blog for current crevasse/rockfall beta before the trip

climate.typical: Maritime alpine climate with a short weather window; snow can linger on the approach into July and return by early October

bySeason.fall: September brings drier, more stable weather but a more open glacier — NPS conditions reports note extensive crevassing and exposed blue ice by early fall
bySeason.spring: Trail typically still snow-covered; Cascade River Road often still gated
bySeason.summer: Best conditions July–August: meadow trail mostly snow-free, glacier still largely snow-covered and easier to cross, though afternoon buildup/thunderstorms are possible
bySeason.winter: Road closed; route inaccessible without a full winter/ski mountaineering approach

climate.forecastZone: Check the NPS Boston Basin/Cascade Pass climbing-conditions blog and a Sahale-specific mountain weather forecast before the trip; NWAC does not issue summer avalanche forecasts here

climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-Cascades rain-shadow climate typical of the Chelan/Entiat Mountains — less precipitation than the west-side Cascades, but high-elevation snow can persist in the col and summit gullies into July and returns by October.

bySeason.fall: Good class 3 scrambling conditions persist into October, with larch color in the basins below Emerald and Saska as a bonus, but expect overnight freezes and the possibility of early snow.
bySeason.spring: Essentially a winter snow climb through May in most years, with avalanche and steep-snow hazard on the southwest face; attempted mainly by ski-mountaineers.
bySeason.summer: Prime window from mid-July, once the col and gullies clear of snow, through August; the lower valley approach is hot, dry, and largely exposed through old burn areas.
bySeason.winter: Full winter mountaineering/ski-mountaineering conditions and serious avalanche terrain; a documented February 2020 ascent via the Grouse Creek/southwest-face line is described as a probable first winter ascent.

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC zone covers the Entiat drainage directly; the nearest reference is the East Slopes Central Cascades avalanche advisory, supplemented with an NWS point forecast for the North Fork Entiat.

climate.fall: September is possible but the connecting Corkscrew-route glacier becomes increasingly broken later in the season.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists on the approach and connecting glacier; the route is generally not in condition until it clears.
climate.summer: July and August are generally the most reliable months.
climate.winter: Not a winter rock objective; heavy snow and avalanche hazard on approach.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet, heavy Cascade snowpack lingers into early summer on the approach; conditions dry out through August before fall storms return around October.

bySeason.fall: Early storms can bring new snow to the upper mountain by October; days shorten fast.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack; avalanche terrain on the approach slopes -- not a typical climbing season.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Sep); the face/route is normally dry and in condition by mid-to-late July.
bySeason.winter: Not a standard climbing season; heavy snow and avalanche hazard dominate.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North zone (approximate -- confirm current zone/forecast on nwac.us before a trip)

climate.fall: Shortening days and early snow return by October; access-road washouts and wet weather become more likely.
climate.spring: Deep, often unstable snowpack persists into May-June on the approach and glacier; ski-mountaineering ascents are done in April when the road/trail retain consistent coverage for skinning.
climate.summer: Best climbing window, roughly June-September, once the trail and ridge are mostly snow-free, though the summit glacier and final snow slopes persist year-round.
climate.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche hazard on approach slopes; road access toward the trailhead is not maintained.
climate.typical: Wet, marine-influenced Cascades weather — Pacific frontal systems bring fast-moving cloud, wind, and rain even in summer dry spells; the open ridge crest has little shelter from wind.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes); NWAC "West Slopes North" avalanche forecast zone

climate.fall: Climbable after Labor Day in good years, but with shorter days and increasing chance of early-season snow on the ridge.
climate.spring: Highway 20 is often still closed or only recently reopened, and the ridge typically still holds snow/ice into June.
climate.summer: July through September is the prime season; the ridge is usually mostly snow-free.
climate.winter: Highway 20 is closed for the season, making the route inaccessible.
climate.typical: Warm, dry alpine-continental summer days with cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are a documented hazard on this long, exposed ridge.
climate.forecastZone: NWS East Slopes Washington Cascades / Okanogan County point forecast.

climate.fall: Rain returns and temperatures drop; road access can still be fine into October.
climate.spring: Wet, with lingering snow on the access road into May/early June.
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window and the best time for rock climbing on this line.
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall typically makes Hannegan Pass Road impassable to vehicles; this is when climbers park at the Shuksan Picnic Area where the road leaves the highway and walk a fraction of a mile up the road to use the wall for dry-tooling.
climate.typical: Wet, temperate maritime climate with heavy winter snowfall and a relatively short dry-and-mild summer window.
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades / Mt. Baker area (western Whatcom County)

climate.fall: September climbing is possible but the connecting glacier on the Corkscrew descent becomes increasingly broken/crevassed and early-season storms can arrive.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists on the approach and connecting glacier; the technical rock is generally not in condition until snow clears.
climate.summer: July and August are generally the most reliable months, once heather ledges and approach snowfields have melted out.
climate.winter: Not a winter rock objective; heavy snow and avalanche hazard on the approach and face.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet, heavy Cascade snowpack lingers into early summer on the approach; conditions dry out through August before fall storms return around October.

bySeason.fall: Early storms can bring new snow to the upper mountain by October; days shorten fast.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack; avalanche terrain on the approach slopes -- not a typical climbing season.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Sep); the face/route is normally dry and in condition by mid-to-late July.
bySeason.winter: Not a standard climbing season; heavy snow and avalanche hazard dominate.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North zone (approximate -- confirm current zone/forecast on nwac.us before a trip)

climate.fall: Rain returns and temperatures drop; road access can still be fine into October.
climate.spring: Wet, with lingering snow on the access road into May/early June.
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window and the best time for rock climbing on this line.
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall typically makes Hannegan Pass Road impassable to vehicles; this is when climbers park at the Shuksan Picnic Area where the road leaves the highway and walk a fraction of a mile up the road to use the wall for dry-tooling.
climate.typical: Wet, temperate maritime climate with heavy winter snowfall and a relatively short dry-and-mild summer window.
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades / Mt. Baker area (western Whatcom County)

climate.fall: September climbing is possible, with earlier-arriving storms and an increasingly broken connecting glacier on the Corkscrew descent as risk factors.
climate.spring: Snowmelt in the lower gully and approach basin can complicate the route; generally attempted after the gully clears.
climate.summer: July and August are the most reliable months.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; heavy snow and avalanche hazard on approach.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet, heavy Cascade snowpack lingers into early summer on the approach; conditions dry out through August before fall storms return around October.

climate.fall: Cooling temperatures with increasing storm frequency into September-October
climate.summer: Warm and mostly dry, with occasional afternoon thunderstorm buildup
climate.winter: Cold and snowbound; highway access to the trailhead is closed
climate.typical: Dry, continental east-Cascades climate, receiving notably less precipitation than the west side of the range crest
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ522/523 (Upper/Lower Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest)

climate.typical: High-elevation glacier climate on an isolated volcano with no surrounding terrain to block wind; expect below-freezing overnight temps at high camp even in midsummer, intense UV/glare off snow, and fast-forming lenticular cloud caps that signal an incoming front.

bySeason.summer: Best window is July into early August, after the Railroad Grade snowfields consolidate but before late-season crevasses open up; snowmobiles may still be on the lower trail into June.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective for this route — heavy snow loading, avalanche hazard on the moraine/glacier approach, and a long approach in the dark.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "West Slopes North" zone (nwac.us) covers the Mount Baker area.

climate.typical: An above-treeline granite basin and ridge between roughly 7,000 and 8,600 ft on the east side of the Cascade crest; north-facing approach gullies can hold snow into July.

bySeason.summer: Generally warm and dry on the east side of the range, but afternoon thunderstorms build over the Stuart Range in summer — start early and plan to be off the exposed ridge/block by midday.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — deep snow and avalanche-prone approach gullies; the standard route is a summer rock scramble.

climate.forecastZone: No NWAC avalanche forecast covers this east-side rock objective; use a point forecast for Sherpa Peak or the general Stuart Range/Alpine Lakes zone forecast.

climate.summer: Clearer, more stable skies as Pacific high pressure strengthens; this is the standard climbing season for the route.
climate.winter: Cloudy with heavy snowfall; technical routes become serious mixed/avalanche-terrain undertakings and are rarely climbed.
climate.typical: Dry continental east-Cascades climate; the Stuart Range crest catches more precipitation and lingering snow than the Teanaway side. Rock is typically dry by mid-to-late July.

bySeason.fall: Cool, stable weather into September/early October but shorter days and possible early snow
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered through June; not a rock-climbing season
bySeason.summer: Prime season July-August; afternoon thunderstorms are common on the crest
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible; road to Esmeralda gated by snow

climate.forecastZone: NWS East Slopes Central Cascades and Passes; NWAC Cascade East Central for shoulder-season snow

climate.typical: The north-facing basin retains snow later into summer than the south-side approaches, giving a shorter dry-rock window.

bySeason.fall: Climbable into September in a dry year but days are short
bySeason.spring: Snowbound, road gated
bySeason.summer: Best window July-August; afternoon thunderstorms common
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible

climate.typical: Dry continental east-Cascades climate; the Stuart Range crest catches more precipitation and lingering snow than the Teanaway side. Rock is typically dry by mid-to-late July.

bySeason.winter: Inaccessible; road to Esmeralda gated by snow

climate.forecastZone: NWS East Slopes Central Cascades and Passes; NWAC Cascade East Central for shoulder-season snow

climate.typical: Warm, dry alpine-continental summer days (60s-70s F at the highway, noticeably cooler and windier above treeline) with cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common and snow can fall above 7,000 ft in any month.
climate.forecastZone: NWS East Slopes Washington Cascades / Okanogan County point forecast; NWAC covers avalanche and spring snow conditions for early-season approaches.

climate.summer: Warm with afternoon thunderstorm potential
climate.winter: Road closed
climate.typical: Dry summers, closed-road winters
climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes Cascades (winter/spring); point forecast for summer

climate.fall: Face increasingly bare/icy with rockfall risk by fall; not a typical fall objective
climate.spring: Deep snowpack persists into June; best firm-névé conditions on this face are often in late spring/early summer
climate.summer: June-early August typically offers the firmest névé before the face bares out
climate.winter: Inaccessible approach road and avalanche hazard make this a non-objective in winter
climate.typical: Wet, marine-influenced Cascade climate with heavy winter snowpack and drier, warmer summers
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes Central (Skagit River to south of I-90)

climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades alpine climate: heavy winter/spring snowpack, a relatively short and unpredictable weather window in summer, and frequent Pacific frontal systems that can bring rain or snow at any elevation with little warning.

bySeason.fall: September can still go but rock and gully snow degrade further, increasing rockfall/looseness; shorter daylight extends the already long approach days.
bySeason.spring: Deep, often unstable snowpack and difficult/impassable creek crossings on the approach; road/trail access frequently limited by residual winter damage.
bySeason.summer: July-August offers the most consolidated snow on the glacier approach and the most stable rock in the summit gully; still expect afternoon thunderstorm risk.
bySeason.winter: Essentially inaccessible for climbing given the multi-day approach, avalanche hazard, and the FR 26 road closure (Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028).

climate.forecastZone: NOAA Zone Forecast: West Slopes North Cascades (WAZ567)

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet, heavy Cascade snowpack lingers into July on the approach and glacier; conditions dry out through August before fall storms return around October.

bySeason.fall: Early storms can bring new snow to the upper mountain and glacier by October; days shorten fast.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack; avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and glacier — not a typical climbing season.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Sep); the glacier still bridges crevasses better early season, opening up more (and getting more broken) later.
bySeason.winter: Not a standard climbing season; heavy snow and avalanche hazard dominate.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North zone (approximate — confirm current zone/forecast on nwac.us before a trip)

climate.typical: Maritime Cascade weather — cool and often wet or cloudy even in midsummer, with conditions that can change quickly on the glacier; the Neve Glacier holds snow well into August.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (Mount Baker Highway/North Cascades Highway corridor) is the closest published avalanche/mountain-weather zone for early-season conditions.

climate.spring: High avalanche risk, heavy snow at elevation, unreliable access

climate.winter: Not recommended; extreme snow accumulation, avalanche hazard, poor visibility

climate.fall: Narrow late-season window; glacier crevasses open up and weather turns unsettled by late September
climate.spring: Still deep in snow/avalanche season on the Redoubt Glacier approach; not typical for this route
climate.summer: Primary climbing season once the glacier approach has consolidated (Jul-Sep); still subject to sudden rain and fog
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible/expedition-only; a first winter ascent of the west ridge (via a different, Ross Lake/Perry Creek approach) was made Dec 27-29, 2023 at WI2 M5
climate.typical: Cool, wet maritime-influenced alpine climate typical of the North Cascades crest; snowpack lingers into July at these elevations and glacier travel is involved on the approach.

bySeason.fall: Early fall can offer stable, cool conditions but new snow on the summit rock becomes a real risk by late September.
bySeason.spring: Heavy snowpack on the glacier and approach trails; not a typical climbing season for this route.
bySeason.summer: Best window (mid-July–September): most reliable snow-free rock and manageable glacier crossing, though afternoon thunderstorms and smoke from wildfire season are possible.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions with rime ice and deep snow on approach; only attempted by a handful of parties (first winter ascent Dec 2023).

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "West Slopes North" zone (nearest available official avalanche/mountain-weather forecast, though this specific peak is beyond NWAC's most detailed coverage).

climate.summer: Short weather windows are typical for the Northern Pickets; the first-ascent party found useful lingering snowpack easing travel in early July.
climate.winter: The approach road and trail are effectively closed by snow in winter; FR-32 carries a standard gate closure roughly November-March.
climate.typical: Wet, snowy North Cascades maritime alpine climate; snow lingers on the Easy Ridge/Challenger Col approach well into July most years.

bySeason.summer: Mid-July through early September is the only realistic window; both known ascents (2006, 2022) were done in this stretch, but conditions vary year to year and the route can still be wet or snow-covered after storms.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "West Slopes North" (Mount Baker area) for avalanche/winter forecasting; no dedicated summer alpine rock forecast zone identified

climate.typical: Wet, temperate west-Cascades maritime climate; the basin's north-facing aspect and the deep Headlee Pass slot hold snow later than surrounding terrain, often into July.

bySeason.fall: Good cool-weather scrambling into September and early October before the first snow returns to the upper basin; daylight shortens quickly.
bySeason.spring: Can be climbed as a snow scramble while the approach is still snow-covered per Mountaineers guidance, but requires solid ice axe/crampon skills for the steep pass approach.
bySeason.summer: Prime season once the trail clears, typically mid-to-late July onward; can be hot and buggy lower in the valley, with lingering firm snow possible on shaded upper slopes into July.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche-prone slide-alder terrain in the approach gully to Headlee Pass; not a reasonable winter objective for most parties.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC/NWS Central Cascades - West Slopes forecast zone

climate.fall: Increasing storm frequency and cooling closes out the ski-mountaineering season.
climate.spring: Prime season for this route; corn-cycle timing matters for stability and rockfall on the descent.
climate.summer: Face reported to be mostly bare, loose rock rather than a snow climb.
climate.winter: Full winter avalanche conditions; road access itself may require ski/snowmobile.
climate.typical: Deep maritime snowpack persists into early summer at this elevation.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West-slopes North Cascades avalanche zone; NWS Zone WAZ567

climate.fall: First significant snow typically by October; road and route conditions deteriorate quickly.
climate.spring: Snow-covered through June; wet-slide and cornice hazard on the Cache Col snowfields and glacier approach.
climate.summer: Best climbing window (Jul-Sep); afternoon thunderstorms are a recurring hazard.
climate.winter: Road closed, deep snowpack, and avalanche terrain throughout the approach.
climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters and a short, dry alpine summer window; heavy maritime snowpack lingers into July at this elevation.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes); NWAC West-slopes North Cascades avalanche zone for winter/spring conditions

climate.fall: Rain returns and early-season snow is possible at this elevation.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on north-facing slopes and in the approach gully well into early summer.
climate.summer: Warmest and driest period; July-September is the recommended climbing window.
climate.winter: Heavy snowpack and avalanche-prone terrain; not a winter/spring objective for this route.
climate.typical: Wet, heavy-snow Cascade winters give way to a fairly short snow-free window at this elevation; even in summer, permanent ice/snow patches persist on the north and east slopes of Spire, Gunn, and Merchant peaks.

bySeason.fall: Cooler, often clearer weather into October; brush dies back which can ease the bushwhack, but expect wetter rock and shorter daylight.
bySeason.spring: Heavy snow cover and avalanche hazard typically make this a poor scrambling objective.
bySeason.summer: Best window (roughly late July-September) for snow-free brush and rock, though shaded gullies and north/east-facing terrain near the summit can still hold snow or verglas.
bySeason.winter: Not a scrambling objective — deep snow, avalanche terrain, and a long approach.

climate.forecastZone: No NWAC zone forecasts this peak directly; the Stevens Pass zone is the nearest reference point for regional snowpack trends in the shoulder seasons (this is primarily a summer/fall scramble, so avalanche forecasts mainly matter for early/late-season snow lingering on the approach and summit ridge).

climate.fall: Deteriorating weather, increasing snow at elevation, shorter daylight
climate.spring: High avalanche risk, heavy snow at elevation, unreliable access
climate.summer: Best conditions July-August with rare weather windows; afternoon thunderstorms common; temperatures range 30-50F at summit
climate.winter: Not recommended; extreme snow accumulation, avalanche hazard, poor visibility
climate.typical: Alpine climate with significant weather variability
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center forecast for North Cascades

climate.fall: Cools and can turn wet/snowy after September.
climate.spring: Snow/ice can linger into June; SR-20 may still be closed.
climate.summer: Warm and often hot at lower elevations.
climate.winter: Highway closed for the season.
climate.typical: Dry, generally stable summer weather from late June through September; afternoon thunderstorms possible.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes North Cascades / Washington Pass area

climate.fall: Cools and can turn wet/snowy after September.
climate.spring: Snow/ice can linger into June; SR-20 may still be closed for the season.
climate.summer: Warm and often hot at lower elevations — one reason this shaded crag is popular.
climate.winter: Highway closed for the season; crag inaccessible by road.
climate.typical: Dry, generally stable summer weather from late June through September; afternoon thunderstorms possible.
