climate.fall: Season likely ends with the first significant snowfall, typically by October.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack likely lingers into June/July, probably longer on this shaded north aspect than on the SW Route.
climate.summer: Most plausible window, July-September, though a north-facing alpine rock route in this range should be expected to hold snow/ice later than the SW Route.
climate.winter: Not viable.
climate.typical: High alpine maritime climate with rapid weather changes typical of the North Cascades.
climate.forecastZone: NOAA/NWS North Cascades zone forecast; NWAC for snowpack in shoulder season

climate.fall: Cools and can turn wet/snowy after September.
climate.spring: Snow/ice can linger into June; SR-20 may still be closed for the season.
climate.summer: Warm and often hot at lower elevations.
climate.winter: Highway closed for the season; crag inaccessible by road.
climate.typical: Dry, generally stable summer weather from late June through September; afternoon thunderstorms possible.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC East Slopes North Cascades / Washington Pass area

climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-of-the-crest summers with warm days and cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August and are a real hazard on the open ridge and summit. Snow can linger in shaded gullies and on Cooney Pass into July, and early-season snow can dust the summit again by late September/October.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in Merchants Basin and around Cooney Lake in late September/early October — a popular but cold-weather window; watch for early snow on the ridge.
bySeason.spring: Trailhead access roads and the upper trail are typically still snowed in; not a recommended season.
bySeason.summer: Prime window; expect afternoon thunderstorm risk and mosquitoes at Cooney/Martin Lakes into mid-July.
bySeason.winter: FR 4340 is not maintained/plowed in winter; a remote, unforecast objective best avoided.

climate.forecastZone: Outside NWAC's coverage area (NWAC forecasts stop west of the Cascade crest); this is a snow-free-season objective rather than a winter/avalanche route — check Okanogan-Wenatchee NF alerts and a general point forecast instead.

climate.typical: Wet, maritime Cascades climate with some of the heaviest snowfall in North America (the adjacent Mt. Baker Ski Area recorded a world-record 1,140 inches in the 1998-99 season); weather can change quickly on the exposed summit plateau.

bySeason.fall: Cooler, clear high-pressure days are common in September; the first significant snowfall can close the road any time from late September into November.
bySeason.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack often keeps the SR 542 road closed into June; when open, expect snow patches on the switchbacks and possible cornices on Table Mountain's north side.
bySeason.summer: Prime season (July-Sept); north-facing sections can still hold snow into early July; warm, often clear mornings with afternoon cloud buildup over Baker and Shuksan.
bySeason.winter: Road unplowed and gated below Artist Point; Table Mountain becomes serious avalanche and backcountry ski/splitboard terrain, not a hiking objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker Area zone forecast (nwac.us)

climate.fall: Not typically climbed; couloir usually bare rock/scree
climate.spring: Prime ski-mountaineering season — firm morning corn snow, softening by midday
climate.summer: Couloir can bake out to bare ice/scree by mid-to-late summer; glacier crevasses open up
climate.winter: Deep, unstable maritime snowpack; road access typically snow-gated
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate; spring corn-snow cycles are the target conditions for this route
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (approximate — the peak sits near the maritime/continental boundary on the Cascade crest)

climate.fall: Cooler, more stable weather in September can be excellent, but shortening days and the first fall storms narrow the safe window.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack, high creek crossings, and avalanche danger on the approach slopes make this a non-standard season for the climb.
climate.summer: The prime climbing window — the SE gully/chimney rock is driest and the col approach carries less snow, though a firm snow slope below the col often persists into July.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible for this route; deep snow, avalanche hazard, and the long unmaintained approach make it an expedition/ski-mountaineering undertaking rather than a standard climb.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast alpine climate: heavy winter snowpack, wet springs, and a relatively short July-September window of drier weather. Even at the height of summer, temperatures on the summit rarely top 80°F, and freezing nights are possible any month.

bySeason.fall: Can bring stable weather and fewer bugs, but nights get cold quickly and the first fall snows (sometimes as early as mid-to-late September) can make the gully/chimney greasy or icy.
bySeason.spring: Deep snowpack lingers into June on the approach trail and in Thunder Basin; spring ascents are effectively ski-mountaineering/snow climbs requiring full avalanche and glacier-travel judgment.
bySeason.summer: July through September is the only reliably climbable window; the small approach glaciers (Moth, Ten Peak, and neighboring Honeycomb Glacier) are best crossed early-to-mid summer before late-season crevasses open up.
bySeason.winter: Essentially inaccessible — the access road is typically snowed in or storm-damaged, and any winter attempt is an expedition-style undertaking.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone is the nearest published avalanche forecast, though Tenpeak sits close to the Cascade crest between the Stevens Pass and Cascade East zones, so treat forecasts as approximate for this specific basin.

climate.typical: Wet, maritime Olympic climate — the trailhead sits low (~700-1,000') but the route quickly gains into a snowbound alpine environment; expect heavier snowpack and later melt-out than nearby Cascades routes at similar elevation

bySeason.fall: Feasible but increasingly cold and wet; shortening days and early snow can strand parties — check the forecast closely
bySeason.spring: Couloir and Hourglass typically still snow-covered; avalanche hazard possible after storms — check NWAC before climbing
bySeason.summer: Snow retreats through June-July; by August the couloir/Hourglass are usually bare, and loose rock/rockfall become the primary hazard
bySeason.winter: Not a standard winter objective — heavy Olympic snowpack, avalanche terrain, and a long approach make it a serious undertaking

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Olympics zone (for avalanche/snow conditions on early-season ascents)

climate.fall: Conditions deteriorate through September-October as the first snow arrives
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the slope below Sawtooth Pass and on the ridge into June
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window (Jul-early Sep); roughly 5 rain days per month; wildflowers in bloom
climate.winter: Heavy snow; not a season for this route
climate.typical: Wet, mild winters and warmer, drier summers typical of the SE Olympics; snow can linger in the Sawtooth Pass/Gladys Divide approach gullies into early-to-mid summer.
climate.forecastZone: Southeastern Olympic Mountains / Skokomish-Duckabush drainage

climate.spring: Significant lingering snowpack likely on approach and ridge; avalanche hazard present into early summer
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable snow-free window for scrambling per multiple regional route descriptions
climate.winter: Heavy snow typical; road access to the trailhead and the approach trail itself become winter travel/avalanche terrain
climate.typical: Royal Basin sits on the northeast, rain-shadow side of the Olympics, so it runs noticeably drier and sees more settled summer weather than the park's west side, though afternoon thunderstorms are still possible in high summer.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' zone (nwac.us) for mountain weather; no Needles-specific microforecast exists

climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades snowpack. Consistent snow cover typically begins around 5,500 ft and the Colonial/Neve glacier basin holds snow well into midsummer in average years.

bySeason.fall: By September, rock and glacier ice are increasingly bare and hard, with earlier-season snow bridges gone — expect more careful crevasse routefinding.
bySeason.summer: Best window for the route; crevasse bridges on the Neve Glacier are firmest in early morning and weaken through the day, so plan a pre-dawn start.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone, though NWAC avalanche forecasts only run mid-November through mid-April, outside this route's typical Jul-Sep climbing season.

climate.fall: Good scrambling conditions can continue into October in dry years, but road/trail access can close abruptly with early snow
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists on the approach gullies and north-facing slopes, often into July
climate.summer: The prime window (July-September) once gullies have melted out, though wildflowers/meadows peak through the season
climate.winter: Road and route inaccessible/snowbound; not a winter objective
climate.typical: Alpine North Cascades climate right on the Canadian border — wet, snowy winters and a short, dry-ish summer window; the exposed ridge catches fast-moving weather off the Nooksack/Fraser valleys.

bySeason.fall: Can still go in good years through September, but shortening days and the first storms/snow raise the stakes on already-loose rock.
bySeason.spring: Approach road and High Pass Trail are usually still snow-covered; the basin below Larrabee's east face holds avalanche terrain.
bySeason.summer: Best (and really the only sane) window — snow typically clears the approach gullies by mid-to-late July and the route stays climbable into September before early snow returns.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — the road is unplowed past Glacier, snowpack is deep, and avalanche hazard is high.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker zone for shoulder-season snowpack; NWS Bellingham-area point forecast for summer weather.

climate.typical: Cool, changeable crest weather typical of the North Cascades; expect a mix of sun, cloud, and fast-moving afternoon showers or thunderstorms even at the height of summer. Snow can linger in the Barrier's crossing gully and on Pyramid's north-facing terrain into July.

bySeason.fall: Early September can still be climbable but daylight shortens quickly and the first snow can arrive by mid-to-late September.
bySeason.spring: Not a realistic climbing season -- deep lingering snowpack and an unbroken, unmaintained approach trail.
bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window, August most reliable; daytime highs in the 60s-70s F at elevation with nights near or below freezing, and possible afternoon convective storms.
bySeason.winter: Not climbed -- heavy snowpack, avalanche hazard on approach slopes, and no trail access.

climate.forecastZone: No summer avalanche forecast applies here (NWAC is a winter/spring product); check the NPS North Cascades climbing-conditions blog and a North Cascades-specific mountain weather forecast for current summer conditions before heading in.

climate.fall: Larch season (late Sept-early Oct) draws heavy hiker traffic to the basin; early snow/ice possible by October.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists into June-July on Aasgard Pass and upper basin approaches.
climate.summer: Prime climbing window (Jul-Sep); can still be hot and exposed with limited shade in the granite basin.
climate.winter: Deep snow and avalanche terrain; not a standard climbing season for this route.
climate.typical: A short climbing season: heavy Cascade snowpack lingers in the north-facing approach gullies and shaded ledges into July, while summers are typically dry under Pacific high-pressure systems; afternoon thunderstorms are possible July-August.

bySeason.fall: Stable weather can continue into September and even early October, but overnight freezes and early snow can arrive quickly at this elevation, and days shorten fast.
bySeason.spring: Deep snow and avalanche hazard on the approach through Temple Canyon; not a typical climbing season.
bySeason.summer: Prime season (July-September); the trail and talus approach are usually mostly snow-free by mid-to-late July in an average year, but watch for afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Not a viable climbing season — deep snow and avalanche terrain throughout the approach.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC does not directly forecast the Enchantments; check the NOAA point forecast for the Snow Lakes/Enchantments area (nearest broader avalanche/weather context comes from the Stevens Pass/Central Cascades zone).

climate.fall: Possible in low-snow years but with shorter daylight and higher chance of early-season snow on the ridge.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack typically makes the traverse impractical.
climate.summer: Jul–Sep is the primary window, when the ridge and any glacier sections are most predictable.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Wet, unsettled weather is common outside the core summer window; loose rock and a serious ridge line make this route especially weather-dependent.
climate.forecastZone: West Slopes North Cascades and Passes (NWS zone WAZ567)

climate.typical: Warm, dry days with cool nights are typical July-September; afternoon thunderstorms build over the crest with some regularity in summer, and the exposed upper ridge/gully offers no shelter from lightning or hail.

bySeason.fall: Late September-early October brings the area's famous larch color and often more settled weather, but nights get cold and an early season snowstorm can shut things down with little warning.
bySeason.summer: Gully snow/ice typically clears by mid-to-late July in an average year; the talus/scree approach is fully exposed to sun, and there is no reliable water source above Snowy Lakes.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC's East Slopes North zone covers the Washington Pass/Highway 20 corridor - mainly relevant for assessing lingering gully snow/ice in the pre- and early-summer season rather than for the dry midsummer climbing window.

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows; snow can return to the high country by October.
climate.spring: Deep, lingering snowpack; Cascade Pass and Pelton Basin are typically snow-covered and NPS will not issue backcountry reservations for trips starting before July 1.
climate.summer: The best and most reliable climbing window, July through September.
climate.winter: Cascade River Road is closed at mile 20; the peak is effectively inaccessible except to ski/snowshoe mountaineers.
climate.typical: Marine-influenced North Cascades climate with a strong crest effect: heavy winter snowpack, wet springs, and a relatively dry, sunny summer window. Because the peak sits near the range crest close to Cascade Pass, weather can build quickly from the west even on an otherwise clear day.

bySeason.fall: Snow can return to the high basins by late September/October, complicated by shortened daylight.
bySeason.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack, high stream crossings below Pelton Basin, and difficult access make spring a poor season for this route.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the reliable weather and access window; warm days with cold nights at Trapper Lake (~4,170 ft) and cooler conditions near the 7,530 ft summit, plus afternoon thunderstorm risk by late summer.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — Cascade River Road is closed well below the trailhead and the trails are snowed in.

climate.forecastZone: Outside NWAC's routine avalanche-forecast coverage; the closest usable proxy zones are NWAC's East Slopes Central and NWS Cascades-East mountain weather forecasts, but treat both as approximations for this Stehekin-side terrain.

climate.fall: Often settled and clear early, with storms returning through October. The road closes with the first heavy snowfall.
climate.spring: Deep snowpack lingers into June. Wet-loose avalanche cycles run off the cliffs above Snow Lake on warm days and cornices along the Tatoosh crest are large. Stevens Canyon Road is usually still gated until around Memorial Day.
climate.summer: Driest and most settled season, with generally clear skies — but the ice route is long gone and the northwest face is running water and loose rock.
climate.winter: Cloudy, wet and snowy, with heavy accumulation. This is the only season Fantasy Falls forms, and also the season the access road is closed. Avalanche danger in the approach drainage is the dominant planning factor.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Weather fronts off the Pacific track northeast into the Cascades and are forced up by the range, dropping heavy precipitation — snow in winter. Temperatures are moderated by the ocean and rarely exceed 80F or drop below 0F.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes South (Mount Rainier area); nearest telemetry is the NWAC Paradise station at about 5,400 ft. NWAC issues avalanche forecasts roughly late November through mid-April.

climate.spring: Deep snowpack persists into June; Thunder Creek runs high and cold with snowmelt.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season (Jun-Sep in trip reports); glacier crevasses and moats open progressively through the season; afternoon wet-slide potential on sun-exposed snow.
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall and avalanche hazard; access road (SR-20) closes seasonally near Ross Dam/Diablo Lake.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the North Cascades crest: wet, heavy-snow winters that build a deep, avalanche-prone snowpack on the approach slopes, and drier summers with more reliable clear-sky windows for glacier travel.

bySeason.fall: Early-season snow can return by October, re-covering crevasses in a dangerous half-bridged state and making route-finding on the southwest slopes harder.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack and avalanche hazard on approach slopes.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the most reliable glacier-travel window, though crevasses have become more exposed in recent years as the McAllister/Klawatti/Borealis Glaciers retreat; afternoon thunderstorms are possible.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "West Slopes North" avalanche/mountain-weather zone covers this part of the range for spring conditions; NWAC issues daily forecasts roughly mid-November through mid-April.

climate.typical: Maritime Cascade-crest weather typical of Stevens Pass — one of the snowiest highway passes in the Cascades in winter, and prone to wind, fog, and afternoon showers even in summer. Check the NWAC mountain weather forecast for the Stevens Pass zone before heading up.

bySeason.fall: September and early October usually offer the driest, most stable footing before the first snow returns to the crest.
bySeason.summer: July can still hold snow patches on north/shaded aspects and the brush is at its thickest and wettest; slopes are mostly dry and open by August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (avalanche forecasting there runs late fall through spring only; NWAC is inactive in summer, so check general mountain weather instead for a Jul-Oct scramble).

climate.fall: September-early October: Temperatures dropping (45-60 F day, 25-35 F night). Morning frost common. Increasing storm frequency. Late October: Significant weather deterioration, early snow possible at higher elevations above 7,000 feet.
climate.spring: Snow present at lake level through mid-June in most years. Cold temperatures (freezing at night, 30-40 F during day). Avalanche danger on the steep approach above Upper Snow Lake. Not recommended for climbing.
climate.summer: Best and most stable season (July-August). Daytime temperatures 55-70 F, nights 35-45 F. Low precipitation, clear skies common. Occasional afternoon thunderstorms. Ideal climbing window.
climate.winter: Deep snow and avalanche terrain make the basin a winter travel/ski objective only — not accessible for rock climbing.
climate.typical: Alpine environment with rapid weather changes. Temperatures range from 40-65 F during summer days, dropping to 20-40 F at night. Wind is common at altitude. Afternoon thunderstorms develop frequently June-September.
climate.forecastZone: NOAA Forecast Zone: Central Washington Cascades (Leavenworth area)

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows and earlier snow.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists into summer; approach trail may have avalanche debris and high river crossings.
climate.summer: Best climbing window; still expect near- or sub-freezing nights on the approach.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible; deep snow and avalanche hazard.
climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters and a short, roughly Jul-Sep climbing season typical of the western North Cascades crest.
climate.forecastZone: NWS West Slopes North Cascades zone (WAZ567); nearest NWAC backcountry zone is Mt. Baker / West Slopes North

climate.fall: Thin, unconsolidated early-season snow over rock. Not recommended.
climate.spring: Consolidated snow can make for a fast, secure climb early in the day, but the sunlit half of the gully turns to wet-slide terrain quickly once the sun hits it. Early starts are essential.
climate.summer: Out of condition - the gully melts out and there is no route here.
climate.winter: The main season. Cold, settled weather after a storm cycle gives the solid-under-the-surface snow the first ascensionists described; storm days and warm spells do not.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy, wet Pacific snowfall at the pass and frequent warming cycles; temperatures west of the crest very rarely fall below 0 F or exceed 80 F, so rain-on-snow and rapid consolidation-then-destabilization are normal.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass avalanche forecast zone (West Slopes Central)

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows and increasing new-snow risk from September on
climate.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack lingers into June-July on north-facing terrain like this ridge
climate.summer: Best window (Jul-Sep) but afternoon thunderstorms and cloud buildup over the Pickets are common
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall, avalanche terrain, essentially inaccessible to casual parties
climate.typical: Cool, wet, and heavily glaciated even in summer. The Chilliwack River/Whatcom Pass corridor sits under some of the heaviest snowfall in the North Cascades, so the approach trail and Whatcom Pass itself often hold snow later into the summer than approaches further south or east.

bySeason.fall: Shortening days and the first snows can arrive by late September/October; a narrow window after summer melt-out and before winter.
bySeason.spring: High avalanche hazard on the approach and heavy, dangerous stream fords from snowmelt; generally not recommended.
bySeason.summer: Primary climbing season; glacier and moat conditions shift fast through the season — early vs. late summer beta can differ dramatically.
bySeason.winter: Road and trail typically snowed in; not a winter objective.

climate.forecastZone: Washington Cascades - Mt. Baker/Whatcom zone (NWAC covers spring avalanche conditions; NWS Bellingham for summer forecasts)

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows, increasing new-snow risk from September on
climate.spring: Deep unstable snowpack on approach and on the summit snowfield into June-July
climate.summer: Best window (Jul-Sep); afternoon cloud/thunderstorm buildup over the Pickets is common
climate.winter: Heavy snowfall, avalanche terrain, essentially inaccessible
climate.typical: Cool, wet, and heavily glaciated even in summer. The Chilliwack River/Whatcom Pass corridor sits under some of the heaviest snowfall in the North Cascades, so the approach trail and Whatcom Pass itself often hold snow later into the summer than approaches further south or east.

bySeason.fall: Shortening days and the first snows can arrive by late September/October; a narrow window after summer melt-out and before winter.
bySeason.spring: High avalanche hazard on the approach and heavy, dangerous stream fords from snowmelt; generally not recommended.
bySeason.summer: Primary climbing season; glacier and moat conditions shift fast through the season — early vs. late summer beta can differ dramatically.
bySeason.winter: Road and trail typically snowed in; not a winter objective.

climate.forecastZone: Washington Cascades - Mt. Baker/Whatcom zone (NWAC covers spring avalanche conditions; NWS Bellingham for summer forecasts)

climate.typical: Wet, mild winters and springs at the trailhead give way to a short dry-ish alpine window in the high basins; afternoon thunderstorms are common in mid-to-late summer.

bySeason.fall: Short weather windows persist into September before early-season snow returns to the high basins.
bySeason.spring: Heavy snow still covers the Barrier and both basins; not viable for this route.
bySeason.summer: Prime window July-September; snow can linger in the approach gullies into early July, and afternoon convective storms are common in August.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible for this route; deep snow and avalanche hazard on the Barrier and basin approaches.

climate.forecastZone: NOAA Zone WAZ301 (Cascades of Whatcom and Skagit Counties)

climate.fall: Early-season snow possible by late September/October
climate.spring: Deep lingering snowpack and high avalanche hazard on the approach
climate.summer: Warmer and drier July-September, though afternoon thunderstorms occur
climate.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche terrain; route effectively inaccessible
climate.typical: Wet, maritime-influenced alpine climate typical of the North Cascades
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades National Park backcountry / NWS forecast zone for the North Cascades

climate.fall: Often good weather into October but increasing chance of early snow and rain events
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack at elevation and high, potentially dangerous river fords during snowmelt
climate.summer: Best weather window (July-Sept); warm days, cool nights, with some afternoon convective/thunderstorm risk
climate.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche terrain; road/trail access effectively closed
climate.typical: The Olympic interior sits partly in the rain shadow of the range's outer peaks but still receives significant precipitation and fast-changing mountain weather; expect the possibility of rain or thunderstorms even in mid-summer, and be prepared for whiteout/low-cloud conditions on the open upper slopes.

bySeason.fall: Snow-free access can persist into Oct in good years, but storms become more frequent and daylight shortens quickly.
bySeason.spring: Trails and the upper cirque are typically still snow-covered; the long approach makes this a poor season.
bySeason.summer: Jul-Sep is the primary climbing window; daytime temps are mild but weather can shift quickly and afternoon buildups are possible.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective - approach trailheads and roads may be inaccessible, and the route is unmaintained and remote.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' zone covers winter avalanche forecasting for this range but is largely irrelevant to the typical Jul-Sep scrambling season.

climate.fall: Good hiking into September/early October until snow returns; lookout is locked from November.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists on the road and trail well into early summer; access road often not passable to Twin Lakes.
climate.summer: Best window Aug-Sep; can still hold lingering snow on upper slopes into August in heavy-snow years.
climate.winter: Road and trail buried in snow; lookout closed November-May.
climate.typical: Cool, often cloudy and windy alpine climate typical of the west-slope North Cascades near the Canadian border; the exposed summit and lookout catch fast-moving weather off the Fraser Valley.

bySeason.fall: Crisp air and the clearest long-range visibility of the Pickets and border peaks; first snow can return to the upper trail by October.
bySeason.spring: Road usually still gated or snow-covered into June; when accessible, steep lingering snowfields below the summit demand ice axe and self-arrest skill.
bySeason.summer: Warmest and most reliable window; trail is typically mostly snow-free by late July/August, though isolated snow patches and afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
bySeason.winter: Deep snowpack, avalanche terrain on approach slopes, and FS Road 3065 typically ungated/unplowed — access effectively requires a long snow approach or is impractical for most.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker Zone (West Slopes North)

climate.typical: A drier, continental climate typical of the NE Cascades' rain-shadow — noticeably less precipitation than the west-side Cascades, but with strong diurnal temperature swings and summer afternoon thunderstorms that build quickly over the open Pasayten highlands.

bySeason.fall: Good hiking continues through September into early October with larch/aspen color; nights drop below freezing and days shorten quickly; blaze orange recommended during general hunting season.
bySeason.spring: Trail and upper road remain snow-covered into June in most years; FR-39 may still be gated by lingering snow at higher stretches.
bySeason.summer: Prime window from mid/late July through September — hot, dry days, but watch for fast-building afternoon thunderstorms and start early to be off the open summit ridge by early afternoon.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions with unplowed access roads — the area is effectively closed to casual access without a ski/snowshoe expedition.
